estimates.basis: The older John Glasgow who held the Saltmarket Rankin–Young tenement in 1527 is assessed as the probable father of William Glasgow-1098. William occupies the matching parcel by 20 February 1528/29; the later St Andrew prebend rental retains its four-shilling burden, west-side street position and Rankin boundary. The 1534 family settlement and 1564 service as heir then directly identify the younger John Glasgow-1093 as William’s son. Read together, these describe a sustained family title rather than merely two men sharing a surname. Lineal succession from the earlier John to William is the preferred reconstruction, while the last William-to-John step is independently documented. The grade is now probable, below documented or strongly supported. This brings the formal local father assessment into line with the stronger property argument already developed in the research. The missing 1527–1529 conveyance has not been found. No inspected instrument calls William the earlier John’s son, and no recorded ages distinguish father from brother. A brother, collateral heir or purchase from a namesake remains possible. Indeed, the neighbouring Henryson parcel in the 1528/29 instrument passes between brothers; title succession alone cannot specify kinship. The combined parcel descriptions are correlated, and the later rental is not an independent record of the original transfer. Glasgow-1095 remains a provisional representation of the Saltmarket owner: its identification with the Stirling witness or the 1506 alias-Smith purchaser is not proved. The probable grade applies to the property-defined Saltmarket father hypothesis, not to every imported biographical claim. No mother is inferred: Eufame Craig may have been the earlier John’s widow, but this does not establish her as William’s mother. No Stirling parent, birth estimate, death location or identity merge is upgraded. The live WikiTree father flag remains uncertain; probable is a local research grade.

Prefer the existing James Glasgow-991 and Christina Bie-55 family account for the Fisherrow James and Christina Bye. The printed 1624–1625 index explicitly groups James, tailor in Fisherrow and burgess of Musselburgh, his son Alexander and wife Christina Bye; it separately names Alexander’s wife Janet Clerk. Those are the same named family roles already represented by these profiles. The local James account also includes the Inveresk father sequence of 1609–1618, which can continue into the Fisherrow household. The ordinary Bye/Bie spelling and the full family fit make the identification probable, rather than a match resting only on James’s forename. This is an assessment of the preferred existing family account, not independent confirmation from its copied tree fields. The Mid Calder and Inveresk baptism sequences may still represent one mobile father or two contemporaries; no occupation or property recital joins them. The profile’s birth and death places remain inherited claims. The signed-in FamilySearch record VQ4V-K87 was inspected on 17 October 2026: it names William, father James and the 10 July 1614 Inveresk event, but no mother. It therefore supplies no independent evidence for Christina Bie’s maternity, consistent with the FMP and supplied ScotlandsPeople entries. The earlier citation-based claim that this record named her is withdrawn; the underlying parish image remains uninspected. Christina’s 1589 New Aberdour birth is tree-derived. Naming her as James’s wife in 1624 does not establish her as Alexander’s or William’s mother. The Andrew-3163 and Murieston-George ancestry alternatives retain their grades.

Select Robert Glasgow-1027 and Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the uncertain working father and mother of Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, through the existing possible identity with their son Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised at Glasgow on 17 November 1618. The 1653 Larne account gives no age or parents, and its before-1625 birth boundary permits the 1618 child; that child would have been about 23 during the alleged 1641 events and 35 in 1653. The Scottish child has no established later fate that excludes this adult account. Choose the already recorded possible identity as the working family explanation, at low confidence. The baptism names both parents, so the maternal selection is assessed from that same explicit child clause, not from a Cunningham surname association in Ulster. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain identity and remain uncertain; the baptism’s direct parentage must not be transferred as proof of the Larne man’s origins.

Select Robert of Larne-3970 as Captain James Glasgow-3172’s uncertain working father. This adopts the existing possible son-or-younger-relative comparison: Larne, Belfast and Kilwaughter form the north-east Antrim setting of the recorded Robert and later James, and an older Robert active in 1641–1653 can precede a shipmaster active by 1667. James commanded the Blessing of Saltcoats in the 1667 Macartney correspondence and the James of Belfast in 1679. These are compatible Scottish-west-coast/Antrim associations, not a parent clause. Son is selected over the unresolved younger-relative alternatives for one provisional paternal route; no mother is selected for James.

Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of George Glasgow-3100 of Campbeltown through possible identity with John’s indexed Linlithgow son George-1560 of 20 January 1622. A child baptised in 1622 could have been about 37 at Alexander’s 1659 Campbeltown event and about 28 in the approximate 1650 generation assigned to James and Agnes. This is a workable adult generation for the household. Prefer this comparison provisionally over the older 1605 Mid Calder George-1082, who would have been about 54 in 1659, without excluding that man. The 1627 Glasgow George-1090 is a close alternative, about 32 in 1659; his profile also carries a separate, unproved Fanne Smith household association requiring its own identity review. The preference is weak and practical: the 1622 child has no established incompatible adult fate, and the household timing is compatible. Missing later records are not positive identity evidence. No shared occupation, holding, spouse, witness or migration record identifies the Linlithgow child with the Campbeltown father. This is a very low-confidence family selection, not an identified migration or a record naming the adult’s father.

The father selection is low confidence; it does not identify the child with the adult as an established fact.

estimates.basis: Glasgow-2462 is the proposed, very uncertain working father of the traditional Ulster ancestor Glasgow-591 and the Cavers Covenanter Glasgow-4138. This carries the existing possible identity with the Polwarth child Glasgow-1605 into a concrete local family model. The Polwarth index names the child’s father as William Glasgow, and Glasgow-2462 is already attached to that child with uncertainty. The three younger profile accounts are retained as possible stages of one life, not three proved brothers. Neither new father attachment is independent support for the other: both depend on the same child/adult identity and on the unproved identification of the named Polwarth father with the Inveresk man. The Polwarth child was baptised on 4 April 1658. If baptised near birth, he would have been about 21 at the examination of the Cavers servant in June 1679, 26 at the Ormistoun servant list in 1684 and 31 in 1689. Those are compatible ages for the recorded adult and the later military tradition. The Ulster profile’s circa 1656 birth is explicitly a rough grandson-based estimate, not an age stated by a record; its guessed Glasgow-city origin cannot exclude a Borders childhood. The exact forename and surname, compatible sequence and existing Borders candidate make this a usable provisional life model. Polwarth and Cavers are distinct parishes in different counties, and the chronology supplies compatibility rather than an identifying age match. The Cavers setting is recorded residence/association, not a proved birthplace. The Cavers man is the leading existing Scottish comparison for Glasgow-591 because the records establish a Covenanter and wreck survivor before the reported 1689 episode, while a probable member of his actual parish survivor group, James Young, appears among survivors said to have reached Ulster. Waddell’s 1886 account says all fifty survivors reached northern Ireland; his revised 1902 account says only some and omits both Glasgows from its named list. The omission does not exclude William, but the revision and late publication weaken the blanket migration claim. The 1684 Ormistoun record also prevents assuming uninterrupted Ulster residence from 1679. The later family history’s 1689 service and settlement remain tradition, not verified military service. No particular crossing, return journey, unit or Irish residence is invented. Its Cameron-to-Glasgow surname-origin story cannot explain a man already called Glasgow in 1679.

Glasgow-1509, the older Larne ropemaker, is selected as the uncertain working father of Adam of Inishrush (Glasgow-3902). This adopts the named-family comparison already tested in September. Adam’s gravestone age implies birth about 1758; James’s reported 1737 birth would give an ordinary age-21 generation. The original 1773 affidavit independently places the Larne James’s birth before October 1743, although it does not prove the reported 1737 year. Adam’s proved son James (Glasgow-3903) supplies limited positive naming support. James is a documented adult with a trade and property trail, making him a more useful provisional father than the recordless Glasgow-3905 placeholder. No record names Adam as his child, and the naming argument is weak rather than corroboration of a parent clause. A 1760 lease identifies James as a Belfast ropemaker taking a ropewalk at Gardenmore, Larne; the 1768 assignment identifies the same property. This is a real occupational and locality sequence, distinct from the contemporary Larne tanner. Adam is documented much later at Inishrush, and the monument does not state his birthplace. The estimated Inishrush birth cannot exclude a family from elsewhere, but no Belfast birth or Larne-to-Inishrush migration is newly assigned. The 1773 Larne gentleman’s age excludes the younger Glasgow-3991 account; the identity assessment and separation of the two trades retain their previous grades. The reported James/Shutter-46 marriage in 1762 is later than Adam’s birth. It cannot establish Shutter-46 as Adam’s mother. An earlier union, premarital birth or inaccurate reported date would be needed if this father model is right; no such event or person is invented. Shutter-46 is not selected as older Alexander’s mother either: the marriage report and the son identity are independently unproved.

The same James is selected, with very low confidence, as father of the reconstructed older Alexander (Glasgow-3904). This adopts the existing possible-brother route for Adam and Alexander. Adam’s wife Unknown-760890, born about 1766/67 from her monument age, cannot be Alexander’s mother on that chronology. The sibling route is therefore preferred provisionally without inventing an earlier wife. Chronological economy does not prove brotherhood or a shared father; neither selected edge is independent support for the other. estimates.basis: The West Kilbride John Glasgow-3161 is the selected uncertain working father of Rev. Patrick Glasgow-635, through possible identity with the indexed child Patrick Glasgow-3160 of 1700. The minister’s church-history account calls him Patrick, and the previously reviewed biography of his son calls the father a native of Scotland. If the 1700 child became the minister, he would have been about thirty-five when son James was born in 1735, thirty-six when ordained at Manokin in 1736, and fifty-three at his death in 1753. James Glasgow-3332 is the selected uncertain working father of Robert Glasgow-3407, who married Katherine Wilson at Carnwath in 1713 and is associated with son John Glasgow-2870 at Libberton in 1722. This is conditional on James representing the weaver at Back of Lindsaylands whose testament was indexed in 1680. The adjacent Biggar, Libberton and Carnwath family setting supplies a specific local comparison. A James born around the inherited 1630/1634 estimates could father Robert in the 1660s or 1670s; a Robert born in the 1670s could marry in 1713 and father John in 1722 at ordinary adult ages. This provisional older-generation route is preferred to making the two overlapping Libberton Roberts sons of the same Johne. No record names Robert as the weaver’s child. Robert’s current circa-1690 birth estimate would be too late for a father dead by 1680; an earlier birth is required if this hypothesis is right. That estimate is unsupported, but the required revision remains a limitation, not evidence for the proposed father.

John Glasgow-3375 is the selected very uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3018, treating the latter provisionally as the father named with Agnes Martine in the 1693 Irvine child entry. The route adopts the existing comparison with John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679 as child of John and Barbara Alason. Exact forename and surname, the neighbouring Ayrshire parishes, and a specific recorded child/parent pair make this a usable local model. It is not a merge or an identification of all events currently collected under either account. If the 1679 event was an infant baptism, that child would have been only fourteen by the 1693 entry. This is a serious weakness. Baptism of an older child would allow an older father, but no evidence establishes such a baptism; neither an earlier birth nor unusually young fatherhood is asserted as fact. The current circa-1675 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent support for the match.

John Glasgow-551, the John said in the later family history to have found a home in County Tyrone, is selected as a very uncertain working father of John Glasgow-3960, gentleman of Gortigillagh, County Leitrim, recorded in 1728. This develops the comparison already recorded in both case files. Keeping their current estimated generations separate gives about 1681 for the older John and about 1705 for the witness: a possible 24-year father–son interval. The proposed connection gives the Leitrim household a testable place alongside the early Irish family tradition. Its preference over an identity match depends on retaining those two estimated generations; neither birth year is independent evidence for paternity. The same uncommon surname and an early Irish setting support investigating kinship, but do not determine its degree. There is no named-father clause or documented Tyrone–Leitrim migration, and no place of birth is inferred from this link.

John Glasgow-1065 is selected as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-2467, the John recorded with Mary Auld at Kilwinning for Andrew’s baptism on 26 October 1746 and James’s on 19 August 1750. The later John’s existing biography already suggests descent from John Glasgow-2463, an old parent reference with a 16 September 1683 Kilwinning date. The current captured family fields of the older household’s children point to John Glasgow-1065, whose profile carries that same 1683 date and the Jean Wyllie household. This resolves the intended candidate account; it is not a new historical father statement. A specific route is the recorded John Glasgow-2464, baptised at Kilwinning on 19 December 1703 to John Glasgow and Jean Wylie, residence Chappell. Treat that child provisionally as the later Mary Auld husband. If baptised in infancy, he would have been about 42 and 46 at the two known children’s baptisms, compatible ages for a father. The later profile’s before-1728 estimate permits this earlier birth. Exact name, parish, an already recorded descent suggestion and a documented child with named parents give a testable family model. No record yet establishes that the child and adult were the same man.

James Glasgow-3526 is selected as the uncertain working father of John Glasgow-2847, husband of Margaret Anderson and father of the West Calder children recorded from 1745 to 1755. The route provisionally identifies that adult with John Glasgow-3525, indexed at neighbouring Kirknewton and East Calder on 31 March 1717 with father James. The parish setting, exact forename and surname, and feasible generation favour this concrete local childhood over an unidentified origin: if baptised near birth in 1717, John would have been about 28 in 1745 and 38 in 1755. The later family also contains a James, although a common repeated forename does not independently establish a grandfather. No register entry yet joins the child to Margaret Anderson’s husband. This is a low-confidence identity-based parent model, not a proved father clause for the adult.

Patrick Glasgow-1440, represented by the Gordon Patrike baptism of 1667, is selected as a very uncertain working father of Patrick Glasgow-3920 of the Kilclone memorial. The memorial’s age 60 at death in May 1754 puts the younger Patrick’s birth around 1694. If the Gordon baptism was near birth, the older Patrick would have been about 27 then: an ordinary father–son interval. The matching Patrick/Patrike and Glasgow/Glasco name pair supplies a specific older candidate rather than an invented ancestor. This is a very weak generational model; neither name recurrence nor a feasible age establishes paternity. There is no reviewed deed, parish entry, probate clause, occupation or shared associate connecting Gordon or Stitchel to Kilclone. No migration or Scottish birthplace is newly established for the Meath man, and the catalogue is not a complete census of older Patricks.

James Glasgow-1025 is selected as the very uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2988, the 1766 Corvanaghan householder, through preferred provisional identity with James Glasgow-1024 of Moneymore. The existing Corvanaghan biography already retains the Moneymore man as a compatible candidate: the places are roughly nine miles apart, the name matches and their circa 1720/1722 births are estimates rather than a real two-year conflict. The 1766 Irish occurrence can precede the compiled 1770 immigration claim associated with the Moneymore family; no post 1766 Irish occurrence has been assigned to the Corvanaghan man. This is a weak locality and chronology preference, not proof of emigration or identity. The older James is already an uncertain father in the Moneymore pedigree. Extending that attachment gives the Corvanaghan account a conditional place in the same family, without inventing an intermediate generation. It inherits two major uncertainties: adult identity and the older pedigree itself.

Caleb Glasgow-363 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Lemuel Glasgow-2581. The case combines a local surname household, a compatible older generation and the same Currituck–Pasquotank setting. Lemuel’s November 1833 pension declaration says he was born in Currituck, moved to Pasquotank as an infant and remained there until moving to Randolph about 1803. William Glasgow-428’s previously reviewed 1746 Currituck will names a son Caleb. The two modern Caleb accounts, Glasgow-363 and Glasgow-830, both cite a Pasquotank will of 1803. These details make the established local Caleb family a useful preferred home for Lemuel over an otherwise unidentified father. They do not put Caleb in Lemuel’s infant household or name his parents. The preference for Glasgow-363 is generational: its circa 1726 birth allows a father aged about 27 in 1753; Glasgow-830’s circa 1740 birth would give about 13. Neither Caleb birth is established by a birth record here, and Lemuel himself said he had no age record and only believed he was born in 1753. The younger estimate therefore lowers the second account’s preference without excluding it. No baptism, guardianship, deed or pension statement names Caleb as Lemuel’s father. A collateral connection to Caleb, another local Glasgow father or an unrelated Glasgow immigrant remains possible. This is a low-confidence named-family hypothesis, not a documented father clause.

Glasgow-2868 is selected as the very uncertain working father of Glasgow-395. The preferred model identifies Moores-284’s husband with the Robert Glasgow who acted jointly with Joshua Hartshorn over a Cecil County plantation in 1786, then places him in the local Glasgow-2868–Hartshorne-320 family. The joint Glasgow/Hartshorn association gives a more specific family-network clue than surname and county alone. Robert’s estimated circa 1750 birth also fits James’s circa 1720 generation and the existing Cecil children’s mid-century dates. The Harford family context and Cecil land occurrence concern neighboring Maryland counties. This is a conditional reconstruction, not a father statement in either notice.

The existing father relationship from Glasgow-3012 to Glasgow-3610 is now documented locally for the record-defined 1649 child. The supplied Scotland’s People index, Kirknewton and East Calder OPR 690/10/14, FR 15, names JOHNE GLASGOW as parent of the child JOHNE indexed on 22 April 1649. The preserved FamilySearch VQ4K-X6G account agrees on the child, father, parish and date. These are two presentations of the same underlying register, not independent records. Glasgow-3610 is specifically the adult-father account defined by that entry. No inference from age or surname is needed for that parental role.

The 1641 apprenticeship expressly names Robert as James’s father and supplies the Wester Duddingston association. The 1649 burgess entry repeats William Sclaitter and the exact 16 June 1641 apprenticeship date, securely identifying that son as the Edinburgh weaver James-1150. The indexed Robert Glasgow burial in the same parish on 17 January 1647 is a coherent match to that father six years later. No positively evidenced competing Duddingston Robert has emerged from the held family comparisons. Robert-1027 is a Glasgow cordiner with proved parents but no held Duddingston connection; Robert-4006 is a possible earlier identity of this adult, not evidence of a second local father. Together these positive identity and locality links warrant 91% confident inference rather than retaining a probable ceiling solely for an unattested namesake possibility.

assessment_history.source_basis: Robert Glasgow-1156 is now assessed as the probable father of James Glasgow-1150, the Edinburgh weaver. Grant’s 16 June 1641 apprenticeship names James’s father Robert and places the entry at Wester Duddingston with William Crichtoun and master William Sclaitter. The 20 June 1649 burgess admission repeats Sclaitter’s name and the exact apprenticeship date, securely connecting the recorded son to the adult weaver. The Robert buried at Duddingston on 17 January 1647 fits the father’s name, parish and preceding generation, six years after the apprenticeship and before James’s independent household began in 1649. Taken together, the specific local father and the Duddingston burial favour one Robert over an otherwise unattested second contemporary Robert in that parish. The previous assessment treated the lack of a unique identifier as a reason to stop at plausible; the combined argument warrants probable, while remaining an inference.

estimates.basis: Hugh Glasgow-548 and Margaret McCullough-1964 are assessed as the probable parents of Hugh Glasgow-540, the emigrant whose Pennsylvania will was made in 1827 and proved in 1831. William Melanchthon Glasgow’s family history, p.2, explicitly names the elder Hugh and Margaret as the married parents of John, Robert and their youngest son Hugh, born in County Londonderry in 1739. Page 3 follows this younger Hugh’s household through John, whom the author calls his grandfather, and its emigration in 1796. This is specific descendant testimony about a named family, rather than a parent invented from dates or a shared surname. The younger Hugh’s recorded will independently names the same four sons John, Hugh, Alexander and Robert, and daughter Nancy, within the corresponding Pennsylvania household. That agreement supports the family history’s identification of the emigrant and the reliability of its nearer family relationships. It does not independently name his parents. The explicit family account, consistent household identity and feasible generations together warrant probable parentage rather than leaving the father and mother ungraded. Parentage rests on one retrospective family account; later online copies and family trees are derivatives, not independent witnesses. Its author gives no Irish baptism or marriage source, and its 1824 death claim is contradicted by Hugh’s signed 1827 will and 1831 probate. The 1733 marriage, 1739 birth, older Hugh’s circa-1706 birth and Margaret’s imported vital estimates retain their separate evidence limits. The two adult Hugh Glasgow householders in Tamlaght O’Crilly in 1740 support an earlier local surname generation, but the return supplies no kin or townland. Entry 1272 remains a leading compatible identity for the elder Hugh; collector order beside Ellis and McCullough names is not proof of adjoining homes or of Margaret’s father. No particular 1740 householder or the 1772 subscriber is selected as this man. The 1827 will does not name the testator’s parents or his wife; it therefore cannot independently establish Margaret’s maternity or Sally Blair’s identity. No John-551 parentage, older William/Covenanter ancestry, Cameron origin story, or connection to Adam of Inishrush is upgraded. The two brothers retain their existing links and grades: John-549’s captured confident flags are not counted as new upgrades, and Robert-550’s separate life remains unverified.

assessment_history.source_basis: The existing Moneymore father account, Glasgow-1024, is assessed as the probable father of Robert Glasgow-12 and, by inference through their established brotherhood, Arthur Glasgow-649 and Joseph Glasgow-1543. The catalogue description of David Faris’s 1990 genealogy explicitly identifies the Adams County emigrant Robert (1749–1839) as a son of a James resident at Moneymore. It identifies a particular father and son, rather than offering a same-name local candidate. The family letter of 6 November 1806 printed by Faris names Arthur and Robert as Joseph’s brothers; Joseph’s 1831 will independently identifies Arthur as his deceased brother and the younger Robert as Arthur’s son. These sources distinguish the two Roberts and establish the sibling group to which the father attribution can reasonably extend. Robert’s pension supports the County Derry setting and 1769 migration. The approximate generations are compatible; the circa-1722 birth estimate is not independent evidence. The positive father attribution and established family group together warrant probable parentage, while remaining below documented or certain.

The actual Faris book has now been inspected, rather than only its catalogue abstract. Printed p.11 uses a dotted possible connection from James of Moneymore to the American brothers; p.12 explicitly reports that evidence for Robert and his brothers’ parentage had not been found. James was the author’s identifiable County Londonderry candidate, not an evidenced father. The retrospective Irish pedigree on pp.8–9 and Samuel’s 1824 Pennsylvania will discussed on p.12 identify an Irish sibling group, including William, James and Robert remaining in Ireland, without joining it to the emigrant brothers. County setting, a compatible generation and the existing family tradition keep James a plausible candidate, but cannot sustain the earlier probable father assessment. Robert, Arthur and Joseph’s established brotherhood remains separately supported by the maintained 1806 letter transcription and Joseph’s 1831 will. John of Peters Township remains a probable brother at 83%; Faris p.15 also reconstructs the four brothers from the 1779–1780 tax/probate cluster. These sibling arguments do not identify their father. The 1824 Samuel will has been read only through Faris’s excerpt, not its manuscript. The Irish Robert in that will/pedigree is not identified as the emigrant Robert born in 1749. All mothers, upstream ancestry, life dates and current attachments are preserved; no live WikiTree save or identity merge follows. Exact percentages are subjective pair-specific judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied probabilities.

estimates.basis: William’s 1746 Currituck will expressly names Caleb as his son and Abiah and Elizabeth as daughters. The existing Abiah and Elizabeth profiles share the named father, Currituck setting and compatible childhood generation; neither has a conflicting identity. Their father links are documented. The two Caleb profiles repeat the same FamilySearch identity and later Pasquotank will account, indicating possible duplicates. Both fit William’s named son sufficiently for probable father assessments, but they represent one historical son candidate, not two independently proved sons. The will survives here through a checked published transcription; the manuscript has not been newly inspected. Abiah’s competing 1730/1738 estimates and Elizabeth’s 1741 date are not proved by it. Caleb’s conflicting 1726/circa-1740 births, 1781/1804 deaths and Gregory/Sawyer spouse accounts remain unresolved. The 1803 Pasquotank will does not name Lemuel; his very uncertain selected link to Caleb-363 and alternative Caleb-830 retain that grade. Susanah is William’s named wife, but the will does not establish her as mother of every child; no mother is upgraded. Lowdenner is not equated with the named Sarah or unborn child. William’s own father remains unproved.

The family history explicitly calls John a son of William and introduces Hugh, the Tyrone-born weaver, among John’s sons. These are specific parent statements in a continuous pedigree, not parents supplied from a shared surname. The nearer part of that account identifies the Hugh–McCullough family and the younger Hugh’s Pennsylvania household, whose children agree with the independently inspected 1827 will. That household correlation supports the account’s family knowledge without independently proving the two earlier fathers. With the retained generations compatible and no conflicting parent account identified for these traditional roles, William–John and John–Hugh warrant probable local assessments. The preference is for the particular family-history accounts, not an identification with other same-name Scottish or Irish records. Both earlier father names come from one later family narrative; they are not two independent confirmations. John’s circa-1681 birth is calculated and William’s circa-1655/1656 date is estimated, so neither is corroboration. The 1740 return cannot distinguish the two Hugh householders or name their parents. No contemporary record identifies John-551 or William-591 in these roles. The narrative’s Cameron surname-origin and 1689 military story are unverified and are not used as parentage evidence. William’s selected uncertain Inveresk/Cavers identity and Robert-2462 father hypothesis remain separate. John-3960’s very uncertain placement and the alternative that the two Johns are one person remain unchanged. No mother, wife, new date, migration or exact 1740 identity is inferred.

The nearer part of that account identifies the Hugh–McCullough family and the younger Hugh’s Pennsylvania household, whose children agree with the independently inspected 1827 will. That household correlation supports the account’s family knowledge without independently proving the two earlier fathers. With the retained generations compatible and no conflicting parent account identified for these traditional roles, William–John and John–Hugh warrant probable local assessments. The preference is for the particular family-history accounts, not an identification with other same-name Scottish or Irish records. Both earlier father names come from one later family narrative; they are not two independent confirmations. John’s circa-1681 birth is calculated and William’s circa-1655/1656 date is estimated, so neither is corroboration. The 1740 return cannot distinguish the two Hugh householders or name their parents. No contemporary record identifies John-551 or William-591 in these roles. The narrative’s Cameron surname-origin and 1689 military story are unverified and are not used as parentage evidence. William’s selected uncertain Inveresk/Cavers identity and Robert-2462 father hypothesis remain separate. John-3960’s very uncertain placement and the alternative that the two Johns are one person remain unchanged. No mother, wife, new date, migration or exact 1740 identity is inferred.

estimates.basis: The preferred local working parents of the Duddingston Robert are now Andrew Glasgow and Elizat Stevinsoun, through possible identity with their recorded son Robert-4006. The accepted 1597/8 testament expressly names Robert as Andrew’s son by Elizat and makes provision until he reached age. A minor then can fit the adult generation of the Robert buried at Duddingston in 1647 and the probable father of James the Edinburgh weaver. The retained circa-1582 and 1597/before-1597 dates are estimates or bounds, not two exact birth records in conflict. On the maintained, queried Calder-area reading of Andrew’s residence, this offers a positive named-child family candidate in the relevant broad Lothian comparison. The earlier Archibald/Isobell pair has no record naming the Duddingston Robert as its child. Prefer the recorded Corsoun family as the uncertain route, with both former parents retained as alternatives. The 1598 child and the Duddingston adult remain separate WikiTree profiles with an uncertain identity comparison; no merge is inferred. No holding, occupation, wife or named-relative bridge equates them, and the Corsoun/Calder place reading itself remains queried. A different local Robert, including the separate Ninian-son account Robert-1027, remains a comparison. Ninian’s son keeps his proved parents and is not conflated with Andrew’s named son. Elizat’s maternity is direct for the recorded child only; it is uncertain for the Duddingston adult because it depends on the same identity hypothesis. Archibald’s and Isobell’s biological parentage is not disproved. James-1150’s probable father assessment, all other selected families, and the adult’s existing vital fields remain unchanged. Two modern Robert accounts can represent one historical son; they are not independent evidence for two sons.

Alexander’s 1673 Kirknewton birth/baptism index explicitly names father Alexander Glasgow. The existing Alexander-3118 account is the same-parish man indexed marrying Margaret Smith in 1667, six years earlier, with a compatible father generation and a later Agnes child association in 1677. The exact father name, parish and ordered household chronology together favour that existing adult as the named father. Assess the attachment as probable rather than leaving it ungraded. This is an inference identifying the indexed father with the 1667 adult; the child entry alone does not identify that adult by wife, trade or property. Another Alexander could have fathered the 1673 child. The marriage and baptism supply no inspected cross-reference, and the father’s circa-1650 birth is an estimate, not an age statement. Margaret Smith is not named as mother in the reviewed 1673 entry and receives no maternity upgrade. Andrew-1546 remains an uncertain proposed son of the older Alexander. Alexander-1141 remains an unproved child of the 1673 Alexander; the latter himself remains a possible older father behind the 1721–1732 child series. The 1673 birth/baptism dates, the 1701 and 1705 marriages and the later children’s maternity questions are retained. The older John-3610 father route is not strengthened.

estimates.basis: The accepted Kilwinning parish transcripts name Robert Glasgow and Mary Simson as the parents of Hugh in 1716, George in 1719 and Jean in 1722. The existing 1715 Kilwinning marriage index names Robert Glasgow and Mary Simpson; ordinary Simson/Simpson spelling variation, the repeated parental pair and the ordered 1715–1722 family sequence identify one record-defined household. George and Jean also share Byrehill residence. These records document both parents for each indexed child, not merely a spouse inferred as mother. The three child profiles already represent those checked entries, so their father and mother assessments can be marked documented. These are previously accepted derivative register transcripts and indexes; no fresh original image reading or new record discovery is claimed. The three transcripts derive from one parish register and are not independent sources. Hugh’s transcript has no residence field; Byrehill is not newly assigned to him. The FMP page references and the separately retained ScotlandsPeople references remain literal provider locators. This household proof does not newly identify the adult Robert with the 1678 child, prove ancestry above either parent, or identify any child with a later adult. George’s merchant, Manchester inventor and artillery comparisons remain separate; James-1120 and the later Covington family do not receive a new parentage grade. No date, birthplace, spouse, occupation, live parent field or saved certainty flag changes.

The 1624–1625 sasines identify his wife Janet Clerk, and the 1637 child entry repeats that parental pair. The repeated father, parish, ordered child series and independently named couple strongly support this Alexander as the father in all three entries. This is confident family reconstruction from the combined records, not an assertion that each earlier entry names his occupation or wife. No mother is named in the three reviewed child entries, so their maternal grades stay unchanged. Bessie’s 22 March index date and existing 20 March birth field remain unreconciled; no date is changed. Existing confident father settings for James-3923, Robert-1149 and Allexander-1152 are retained, not counted as new upgrades. Original sasines and parish images were not newly inspected.

Prefer the Glasgow child baptised on 19 June 1614 and the Archibaldus Glasgua who graduated M.A. in 1635 as the earlier identity of the Donegal cleric. The uncommon full name, compatible age at graduation, clerical career and 1639 Irish clerk occurrence form a coherent Scottish-to-Irish career. A baptism in 1614 places him at about 21 in 1635 and 25 in 1639. These are conditional ages, not separately recorded ages. No incompatible parentage or simultaneous Scottish household is identified for this proposed cleric. The other known same-generation Scottish Archibald, the Leith man Glasgow-3078, has a separately traced craft career: apprentice to cordiner Thomas Park in October 1639 and shoemaker/heir in May 1647. That positive career sequence makes him a weaker fit to the 1635 graduate and Irish clerk than the 1614 Glasgow child. It is a ranking argument, not an absolute exclusion or an assertion that a man could never change occupation. The Irish testator is securely the Ramelton/Rathmalton cleric by exact name, residence and profession. Assess his existing George Glasgow and Margaret Steuart parent links as probable, reflecting the probable Scottish childhood identification. The baptism explicitly names both parents, so maternity has its own record basis rather than being inferred from George’s spouse field. No Irish record reviewed names Archibald’s Scottish parents or university. The graduation and 1639 clerk entry do not themselves state the 1614 baptism date. Another Archibald remains possible. This is a preferred combined identity, not documented migration or proof that every early Scottish and Irish occurrence is one man. The quoted baptism witnesses are reused from the maintained reading, not newly checked against an image. Margaret’s own Stewart ancestry, George’s wider family, and the 1647–1661 ministry chronology retain their existing grades.

Betham’s inspected abstract of the April 1673 will of Archibald Glasgow, clerk of Rathmalton, explicitly identifies Thomas Glasgow as his eldest son. Prefer the existing Thomas of Lifford/Raphoe account for that son: the exact uncommon name, the adjacent Donegal setting and the next adult generation fit the independently documented Raphoe-linked court case of 1684, Lifford occurrence of 1689 and Ballindrait/Shannon deeds of 1692–1695. The 1692 Creighton court association and later estate material strengthen the continuity of that adult Thomas account; they are not independent statements of his parentage. The full local and generational fit warrants a probable father link to Archibald. A further unique estate or household identifier would strengthen it, but its absence does not require leaving this coherent family at merely uncertain. Betham gives the son no age, residence, spouse or estate. He could be another Thomas, so the Lifford identification remains inferred rather than documented. The profile’s before-1671/circa-1670 birth estimates are not ages supplied by the abstract or court records and are not used as proof of either identity or exclusion. No maternity is assigned to Thomas from Elizabeth’s status as Archibald’s wife. Nathaniel and George remain Thomas’s separately assessed children; the later Killybegs James and Belfast Captain James are not made relatives by this review.

Select Thomas Glasgow-3556 of Lifford/Raphoe as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3001. Thomas is an established Donegal legal/property actor from the 1684 Raphoe-linked court occurrence through the 1692–1695 Shannon/Ballindrait deeds and the 1701 Exchequer continuation. James belongs to a later dated Donegal account under 1728. The same uncommon surname, regional continuity and compatible succession of legal/property and revenue roles make Thomas a useful preferred existing father account. This extends the recorded Ramelton–Lifford family into the otherwise unattached collector account without inventing an intermediary. It is a regional and generational inference: none of these records names James as Thomas’s son. The record dates are not measured ages. The 1728 entry may carry an earlier deceased or dismissed officer’s balance, so it cannot select a generation precisely. Archibald Glasgow-1101, Thomas’s probable father, remains a concrete older-family alternative: James might be Thomas’s younger brother or another kinsman rather than his son. An unrelated Donegal or wider Ulster Glasgow family remains possible. The Tyrone James Glasgow-1025 and Belfast Captain James Glasgow-3172 are not merged with this collector or excluded solely by their unproved birth estimates and parent fields. No Scottish-to-Irish migration, exact age, mother, spouse or child of James is inferred. Thomas’s existing probable Archibald father and his other children keep their separate assessments.

Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as James Glasgow-991’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule. The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father.

For the working tree only, select William Glasgow-3522 as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant George Glasgow-1099. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William. The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits.

Prefer John Glasgow-3193 of the Corsankell/Kilwinning family as Hugh Glasgow-1603’s uncertain working father. This materializes the leading Ayrshire placement already argued in the maintained five-generation map. The 1571 Corsinkell deed expressly names John as James elder’s son; the earlier Kilwinning tenant appearances are attributed to him as probable. Hugh’s surviving profile account describes an Ayrshire progenitor, his son’s account is centred on Kilwinning, and the following households lie in Kilwinning, Ayr and Kilbirnie. These successive local settings favour the documented nearby family over the existing Mid Calder/Inveresk father attachment, which depends on an online tree and has no movement, household or property bridge. A John-to-Hugh-to-John sequence is compatible supporting context, not a naming rule. Father is selected as a revisable one-generation model, rather than leaving the previously preferred local route only in prose. Hugh remains a tree-derived generation: no inspected contemporary record securely identifies him, names his father or establishes his own c.1600 birth. John’s before-1540 boundary means a birth for Hugh near 1600 would make him an older father, around 60 or more; a grandson or collateral position may fit better. Neither date is changed to fit. An earlier Hugh birth is possible but is not adopted as a new estimate, and no missing person is invented. The 1571 John is documented as a son, while his additional Kilwinning identity is only probable. John’s brother James Glasgow-3921, another local Glasgow family, an omitted generation and the former James Glasgow-991 placement remain alternatives. This is stronger locality reasoning, not a probable or proved father assessment. The 1677 deed-index Hugh, preacher of the gospel, remains an unresolved identity comparison and supplies no evidence for this father choice.

Select James Glasgow-1970 of the Cookstown Mitchell family as John Glasgow-2539 of Gortin’s uncertain working father, through the existing possible identification with John Glasgow-1968. The 1879 Hillsdale history specifically identifies James and his Mitchell wife as parents of John, a farmer near Cookstown. The Gortin account supplies another John in the same Derryloran/Cookstown locality and an earlier compatible father generation. The maintained Hillsdale research already lists Gortin John as a possible duplicate. This is a positive named-son comparison in the relevant family and locality, stronger than an arbitrary father chosen only from the surname. Prefer this existing family as a revisable home for the 17-profile Gortin branch; retain both John accounts separately.

estimates.basis: Assess the Hillsdale record-defined core as probable: James Glasgow-1970 as John Glasgow-1968’s father, Unknown Mitchell as that John’s mother, and James and Mitchell as spouses. The 1879 account explicitly gives those relationships; the 1888 sketches identify the same John–Jane household through sons William and John, their seven-child group and Michigan history. These are detailed late family accounts, not contemporary Scottish or Irish birth/marriage entries. Conflicting Scottish versus Tyrone origins, c.1778 dating and 1844/1848 immigration years limit the life-history reconstruction. The family-role identification is still a justified probable inference, while exact dates and the new upstream/Gortin links remain weaker separate questions. The prior local grades were unknown with saved unmarked parent flags; no already-confident link is counted as a new upgrade.

The accepted Findmypast transcript for John Glasgow’s Libberton baptism on 23 September 1722 explicitly names father Robert Glasgow and mother Katherin Wilson, with residence Sandyburgh: OPR 650/1, page 17, item 3, SCOT/OPR/BAP/4033399. The existing John profile is already assigned to this exact record by the completed person-level audit. Robert Glasgow-3407 is the maintained Wilson-household father account and Katherine Wilson-127539 its mother account. Both recorded parent roles should therefore be documented locally, rather than left as unassessed tree fields. These are two explicit parental names in one baptism transcript, not a mother inferred from a husband’s surname. The existing Carnwath 1713 Robert–Katherine Wilson marriage citation is compatible household context; it is not needed to invent the 1722 parents or to treat every local Robert as the same man. The documented assessment applies to the Scottish child and parents in the 1722 baptism. The later American identity attributed to John—Nottingham, Chester County, and a May 1769 death—remains unproved. The profile’s Bible and burial citations have not supplied an inspected migration, household or parent bridge from Libberton. No American newspaper attribution is reinstated. This does not establish that the American John had these parents. The source supplies a baptism date, not an independently proved birth date. Katherin in Findmypast and Katharin in the retained MyHeritage index are provider spelling variants of the record’s Wilson mother, not two independent maternal confirmations. This review reuses the captured transcript of 3 September 2026; no fresh register-image inspection is claimed.
estimates.scope: Scottish child and named parents in the 1722 baptism; American adult identity remains unproved

estimates.basis: Prefer one household: James Glasgow, indexed with Agnes Waitte at Polwarth on 18 June 1663, is probably the James who fathered the Gordon children John (1666), Patrike (1667), Jean (1671), Robert (1673), Agnes (1676) and Margrat (1679). The father’s repeated full name, the neighbouring Berwickshire parishes, the first child three years after marriage and the orderly thirteen-year child sequence form a coherent family. The daughter Agnes supplies modest naming support; it is not the deciding evidence. The maintained 1702 Gordon marriage citation for Jean also names father James, adding a compatible adult continuation for her. Read together, these favour a single local family over six isolated fathers or an unrelated Polwarth couple. No concrete competing contemporary Gordon James household has been identified in the maintained material. That is the scope of this comparison, not a claim to have exhausted the population. The child indexes explicitly name James as father but omit the mother. Their named-father roles are documented for the record-defined children; identifying that father with the 1663 Polwarth husband is probable. Agnes Watt is separately assessed as probable mother of all six children on the marriage, locality and sustained family sequence. This is an inference, not literal maternity in the indexes; a later marriage or another local James remains possible. Jean’s later marriage and the later adult identities of John and Patrick remain separately assessed. Patrick’s proposed Kilclone son and migration, James’s own John Glasgow-1084 ancestry and the unrelated Kilwaughter James are not strengthened. No original register image was newly inspected: this review combines the previously accepted index entries and maintained citations.
estimates.scope: Named father and child in the Gordon baptism index; Polwarth husband identity probable and later adult identifications separate

estimates.scope: These are exact subjective assessments of complete relationship-and-identity propositions, not measured probabilities. The family letter is undated and unsigned and is read through Albert Rutherford’s published transcription of a photocopy, not an inspected PRONI original. The minister list is a derivative compilation whose independence from the family tradition is unproved. The Scottish adult identities remain possible: neither the letter nor the 1705 baptism supplies a migration, occupation, property or witness bridge between Kirknewton and Tyrone. The letter’s three-son family and second-cousin statement are internally consistent clues from one source, not independent corroborations. Existing people, vital fields and mothers are preserved. Miss Cunningham and Anne Rutherford are reported maternal names, not transferred to existing maternal profiles. The letter’s first-settler story is family tradition, not proof of the first Glasgow in Tyrone or of the surname’s origin.

estimates.basis: The anonymous family recollection printed by Faris on p.9 explicitly gives James Glasgow, husband of Margaret Rutherford, four sons: William, Robert, James who settled near Moneymore, and Samuel who went to America, plus daughter Ellen. The letter-defined father is the family role represented by James-1025. These are specific named relationships, substantially stronger than the contributed-tree and locality summaries used by the earlier percentages. The same full-letter tradition was already read on 20 October; actual Faris pages now confirm its full structure. Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses. James-1024 is reviewed as the letter-defined son who settled near Moneymore. The father James and son James occupy explicitly distinct generations in that account; the earlier possibility that these two family roles were one duplicated adult no longer deserves the same weight. The 78% assessment does not identify the son with the Corvanaghan householder or make him father of the American emigrant Robert. These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris calls the anonymous recollection file5 within PRONI T1959, while Rutherford’s reproduced copy cites T1959/3; retain this reference discrepancy pending archive checking. The 1759 probate index says Drumcarn and names no kin; neither that testator nor the inherited life dates are identified by this reassessment. The letter calls William eldest although the imported sibling birth estimates put him later; those estimates remain unverified. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed.

estimates.basis: John's 1616 Mid Calder childhood, proposed adulthood as the Edinburgh whipman married to Issobell Porteous in 1642, and recorded fatherhood in 1643 place him in a plausible father generation for a man marrying in 1663. A James born roughly 1640–45 would fit that adult's family chronology. This is chronological compatibility, not independent evidence supplied by James's estimated birth year. The first recorded Gordon son is John in 1666. That modestly favours a paternal John. If the 1616 child is the 1642 adult, John's recorded father James also gives a compatible James–John–James–John sequence. These common names provide limited support, and the grandfather echo depends on the unresolved child-to-adult identity; it must not be counted as an independently proved multi-generation chain. The 1642 John/Issobell marriage and the 1643 daughter form a concrete candidate household rather than a father chosen solely from a tree name. The 1652 Anne attribution would extend it into the right period, but currently rests on a FamilySearch tree citation and is not equal-quality parish evidence. The separate 1638 John/Helen Patoune household is a provisional earlier identity, not another independent confirmation of the selected father. James's 1663 Polwarth marriage and the six Gordon children in 1666–79 strongly support his own local adult household. They do not locate his childhood or identify relatives in Midlothian. The chosen John is the best of the examined named father candidates, but the aggregate chance of another father remains greater. No source currently distinguishes him from all reasonable alternatives sufficiently for an upgrade.

estimates.basis: Select James Glasgow (Glasgow-1238), the father recorded with Elizabath/Elizabeth Tait at Stichill, as Robert Glasgow’s possible working father, at 34%. The couple’s maintained marriage citation is dated 25 January 1740; their David and James children are indexed in June 1744 and July 1746. Robert’s estimated 1745 birth fits that family generation and could fall between those events; it is not a dated baptism. Stichill and Eccles/Leitholm belong to the same small Borders district, and the later Swinton entry attributed to the James/Tait couple offers a further local comparison. Robert’s earlier son James supplies a modest naming clue consistent with this father; a common forename cannot establish paternity. The combination favours this existing, record-defined family over the catalogue’s distant Kirknewton candidates, whose apparent proximity came from mapping Leitholm to South Leith. No inspected record names Robert as James’s son. This is a preferred, revisable hypothesis, with 34% subjective confidence, not a measured probability or a confident connection. Robert’s 1745 birth and 8 August 1800 death each have zero attached sources on the inspected FamilySearch tree. Neither date establishes an age or place of birth. The local 1745 estimate is retained unchanged. FamilySearch attaches John Glasgow (1720–1785, GFNP-FS8) and Agnes Spark (1722–deceased, K8CD-HCW) as parents; retain that alternative without treating a contributed tree as documentary proof. The evidential basis of that parent attachment has not yet been reviewed. Do not equate that John with the much older John Glasgow-1057, husband of Agnes Spark-330, from the matching names alone. James’s brother John Glasgow-1444, christened at Stichill in 1708, is another compatible local father-generation alternative with no presently inspected Robert link. An unrecorded local father or another kinship degree remains possible. The Swinton/1740 couple continuity and Robert’s own early life need testing. Elizabeth Tait is not selected as Robert’s mother: her marriage and maternity of other children do not identify his mother. Robert is not merged with an earlier child, and James’s existing older ancestry retains its own uncertainty.

Select John Glasco of Drumearn (Glasgow-2990) as Robert Glasgow-1189’s possible working father, at 31% subjective confidence. The specific reported father name John favours a John comparison over the automated leading candidate James Glasgow-1970. The actual 1766 Derryloran return places John at Drumearn beside two James Glasco households, three years before Robert’s estimated birth. That supplies a real Tyrone father-generation account compatible with the reported origin. John’s circa-1750 local estimate and the contributed father’s 1745 year are both unproved; either permits fatherhood around 1769, and no date is changed to fit. The estimate assesses the whole proposition that the documented householder was the reported father. It is not a rating of the census record, a statistical probability, or a product of the uncertain ancestry above John. There are two unresolved steps: whether the contributed John/Margaret parentage is correct, and whether that John was the Drumearn householder. A common given name, estimated generation and claimed county cannot establish identity. The 1766 return supplies no wife, child, age or parent; the nearby James entries do not identify John’s father. Robert’s Tyrone birthplace is not independently established by the inspected Geneanet page. John’s existing uncertain James Glasgow-2988 father is preserved, with no new support. The Cookstown reward subscriber of 1796 is an unresolved namesake comparison, with Robert Glasgow-3941 the stronger maintained candidate; that notice supplies no parent and is not used as proof that the Martinsburg man lived at Cookstown. The single Geneanet/Ancestry family-tree chain and its repetition in WikiTree are not independent witnesses. Retain another unidentified Irish John as a serious alternative. John Glasgow-3314, associated with Margaret Mill and the West Calder children of 1762–1770, matches both reported parental given names and a viable generation, but has no inspected Robert or Irish-origin bridge. His Scottish baptism and actual West Calder household are distinct facts; an unproved Irish birthplace is not a categorical exclusion. John Glasgow-4179 of Larne also fits the estimated generation; his known Rose Allan marriage does not prove there was no earlier Margaret, but no record connects him with Robert or Drumearn. James Glasgow-1970 has a Cookstown family tradition and a rare Julia/Julia Ann descendant-name resemblance; those are useful regional clues, but do not outweigh the specific reported John father name. If that report is wrong, James or another local man remains possible. No competing candidate is rejected merely for missing fields. No mother is selected: the reported Margaret is not identified with Margaret Mill, Rose Allan or any existing profile, and Nee is not adopted as a verified birth surname. Robert’s wife Elizabeth and every existing child remain unchanged. No merge, vital-field change, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made.

estimates.basis: Select James Glasgow of the 1719 Dalziel record (Glasgow-3523) as John Glasgow-3094’s possible working father, at 41% subjective confidence. This joins the Cambusnethan John-and-Ann family provisionally to the adjacent Dalziel James-and-Samuel family. The positive comparison combines a particular nearby surname household, a viable parent generation, and John’s two currently listed sons James and Samuel repeating the older two given names. Samuel is a more discriminating comparison than John or James alone. The proposed sequence is Samuel to James to John to the later James and Samuel; only the first and last household roles have cited baptismal support. No record names the adult John’s father or shows the 1719 child’s later life. The 41% rates that whole immediate-father proposition, including the child-to-adult identity gap; it is comparative judgment, not a measured frequency or a probability for the complete pedigree. John’s 1770 birth is an uncertain profile estimate, not a baptism or recorded age. If taken literally with 1719 it implies fatherhood at about 51, which is possible and supplies no maternity information. An illustrative John birth in 1750–1770 would give a James age of about 31–51 and a 1790 groom aged 20–40; neither range is adopted as a new date. The 15 March 1719 index date is not independently established as a birthday. The named James may have died young or belonged to another later household. Adjacency does not prove continuity, and an interval of roughly seventy years separates the two parish events. James and Samuel are the currently attached children, not a proved complete or birth-ordered family. Samuel could come from Ann Clerk’s family or another relative; no Scottish naming rule determines the father. The family names and the existing father assignment to Samuel are not independent demonstrations of John’s ancestry. Retain another local James or another unrepresented father, and a collateral relationship to the Dalziel family. Samuel Glasgow-3166 is an alternative direct father if John was substantially older than the 1770 estimate; the ordinary younger-groom generation favours an intervening James, but the absent age cannot exclude an older groom. The earlier Calder Alexander/Clerk-marriage comparison remains a possible wider ancestry route, not a proved direct father: repeated Clerk marriages do not identify Ann’s family or establish a two-century pedigree. Other Scottish James households are not excluded for missing fields, but no comparably specific Cambusnethan–Dalziel and James/Samuel sequence was found in the bounded local catalogue comparison. James’s mother and wife remain unknown. No mother is selected for John, and no relationship is inferred between Ann Clerk and the earlier Clerk women. Preserve the existing ungraded Samuel-to-James father mark and all current child-parent grades, without a confidence upgrade or live save. The 1690s–1794 London pen-cutter comparison for Samuel remains very weak and separate; it supplies no evidence for this family. No person is merged, created or redated.

Select Philip Glasco-146, the provisional elder Dublin watchmaker account, as the probable working father of Thomas Glasco-144 at 67% subjective confidence. The maintained reading of the 1773 advertisement explicitly says that Thomas served his apprenticeship to his father Philip Glasco and subsequently practised in London before returning to his father’s Christ-Church-lane house. Thomas’s 12 December 1773 marriage to Margaret Duffy at neighbouring St Audoen’s supplies a particular same-name adult, same year and immediate locality, rather than a Scotland-wide name comparison. A young tradesman returning to the family business and marrying later that year is the preferred explanation. The later Christ-Church-lane to 20 Ormond Quay sequence supports continuity of the watchmaking business. The separate marriage and apprenticeship evidence together justify preferring Philip to the unsupported Thomas-173 father attachment. The 67% rates the complete profile-level father proposition, including identification of the 1773 groom with the advertised watchmaker and of the named Philip with the elder account. Neither the marriage index nor the Duffy pedigree gives Thomas’s trade, address or father’s forename. The advertisement is reused from the 7 October full-page OCR reading; its original image was not newly inspected. The older Philip account contains some junior events, so the elder/junior distinction remains material. Thomas’s circa 1753 birth is an estimate: age twenty would make completed apprenticeship plus several years in London compressed, favouring a somewhat older adult without establishing a replacement birth year. No date is changed. The rare surname, close locality and year are correlated clues, not independent parent statements.

Select the Edinburgh weaver and burgess James Glasgow-1150 as the probable father of the record-defined 1696 apprentice James Glasgow-4114, at 76% subjective confidence. Printed page 37 names the apprentice’s father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Name, occupation, civic status and Edinburgh setting identify a particular established craftsman rather than just a same-name Scottish father. The maintained 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 burgess cross-reference securely establish James-1150 as a weaver and burgess; printed page 72 also records a James Glasgow, weaver and burgess, taking John Paterson as apprentice on 18 October 1693. The maintained burgess-roll review found one matching admission, although an index cannot rule out another man. This makes James-1150 the preferred father-profile match. The child account itself is defined by the 22 April 1696 entry, so no later-life identification is needed for that child. The 76% is an individual research judgment for the whole father-profile identification, not a measured frequency. The published entry proves a father called James, weaver and burgess; it does not supply his apprenticeship date, wife, home address or age. Another matching craftsman, including a Lindsaylands man who also held burgess rights, remains possible. The circa-1680 child date and circa-1620 father date are estimates, not recorded ages; the nominal sixty-year interval makes late fatherhood relevant but is not a contradiction. James’s 1641 apprenticeship supplies no exact birth year. The younger James’s mother remains unknown: neither Bessie Whyte nor Agnes Duncan is transferred merely because she married the proposed father. The father’s existing probable Robert ancestry and all other family grades remain unchanged.

James Glasgow-4114, apprenticed to William Adam, apothecary, on 22 April 1696, and Thomas Glasgow-3285, assigned to the baxter apprenticeship of 11 October 1699, are selected as probable brothers at 79% subjective confidence. Both entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh. The matching personal name, craft and civic status, in the same register only three years apart, favour one father. Thomas is expressly the youngest son. His 13 November 1684 baptism fits entry at almost fifteen, while the Duffe household has sons James baptised in 1679 and 1680, fitting the 1696 entry at about seventeen or sixteen. This is a coherent sibling group rather than a name-only regional comparison. The 79% assesses the profile-to-profile sibling inference, not a literal brother clause or measured frequency. The apprentice entries do not name a mother, address or the father’s admission date; two matching craftsmen remain possible. Thomas’s apprenticeship-to-baptism identity is a maintained assignment, supported by age and locality rather than a repeated birth date. Do not choose between the 1679 and 1680 James children, merge either with James-4114, or transfer Isobell Duffe as his mother. The 1690 Lindsayland apprentice James-4131 remains a compatible comparison, including the possibility of a cancelled first apprenticeship. If that identity is established, its deceased father must be reconciled with the master appearing in 1693.
estimates.scope: Shared father inferred from apprenticeship descriptions; maternity and baptism-profile identity separately unresolved.

estimates.basis: Select Hugh Glasgow-1499 as the preferred possible father of James Glasgow-1509, the older Belfast/Larne ropemaker, at 52% subjective confidence, replacing William Glasgow-1505 in the local working tree. The archived chronology explicitly places a James, son of Hugh, at New Town/Larne in 1737 and identifies its reported 1762 Janet Shutter groom with that James. Hugh is an independently documented Larne merchant and elder, jointly leasing Newtown property in1736 and dealing with Hugh Shutter in the original1749 mortgage. The later James/Janet account and the distinctive Jane Shutter name in the younger William’s monument fit a recurring Glasgow–Shutter network. These combined named-parent, locality, generation and family-association clues favour Hugh over retaining a William father without a named-son record.
estimates.scope: This is a preferred working identification, not a proved father clause for the adult ropemaker. The chronology is one derivative reconstruction: its1737 child,1762 groom and reported1737–1802 stone must not be counted as three independent confirmations. A different Hugh remains possible. No mother is selected: Ann is not established as the1737 child’s mother by the reviewed account. That is a serious rival explanation: the reported1737 child could have died and the name been used again. It is not a recorded death of that earlier child. Withdraw the categorical earlier inference that the1737 James must have died young. Do not equate the two James profiles, invent a second wife, or infer surviving brothers with the same forename as an established fact. The older ropemaker was already an adult in1760–1761 and over thirty in1773, so he remains distinct from the younger monument/tanner comparison. One selected father is replaced locally. The child-side working branch contains49 retained pre-1850 profile accounts, including James and uncertain descendants; their own grades are unchanged. This is not49 new or proved relationships. The men were already in the same working component, so no component merger or new genealogical connection is claimed. No vital date, place, spouse, mother, identity merge or live WikiTree field changes. Hugh’s own uncertain ancestry and James’s Inishrush descendants retain their prior assessments.

estimates.basis: Prefer Alexander Glasgow-3118 as Andrew Glasgow-1546’s father at 58% subjective confidence, possible. The particular Alexander household is established at Kirknewton by the 1667 Margaret Smith marriage and the father-named Alexander and Agnes entries in 1673 and 1677. Andrew’s 1700 Christian Cook marriage and fatherhood of James in 1702 place his own adult household in the same parish, one generation later. The sustained parish setting and feasible household succession together favour this existing family. Andrew, Alexander and Agnes recur in the descendant branches, providing modest supporting context rather than an independent naming rule. This weighs a specific family against alternatives, rather than inferring fatherhood from surname and estimated ages alone. The 1685 birth is an unsourced estimate. Taken literally it makes Andrew about fifteen at the indexed 1700 marriage and seventeen at the 1702 christening. Those ages are possible, but they cannot independently support the pedigree. A birth earlier in the 1670s or early 1680s would also fit the adult events and Alexander’s family chronology; no replacement birth year is adopted. Alexander’s own circa-1650 birth is likewise an estimate. The argument rests chiefly on the recorded adult households, not on moving either birth date to fit.

The older John was already a married farmer in 1786; the younger account’s approximate 1794 birth fits a child of that household. It is a more specific family comparison than a generic same-surname Armagh or Scottish father. Prefer this direct local lineal model over leaving the later four-child household disconnected from its already identified earlier surname household. The connection is an inference from the combined evidence, not a parent clause or an implication of the connectivity score.
estimates.scope: No source names the younger John’s father. The older man’s purchased property was at Lislea, although he resided at Drumgreenagh; no inspected title chain proves that he and the 1839 farmer occupied the same farm. The 1828 Drumgreenagh John probate-index entry is not treated as a proved death, inheritance or link between them: its document type, individual identity and surviving text remain unresolved. Nathaniel-4014 is another older local relative and possible father; an uncle, other collateral, another John, or another unrepresented father remains possible. Both 1786 adults lack recorded ages. The younger John’s 1794 birth is uncertain and has no recovered primary age source in this review, so it cannot absolutely exclude his being the 1786 man at an older age. The preferred father model keeps the two accounts separate without claiming that distinction proved or merging them. Jane Murphy is the older John’s documented wife, but is not assigned as the younger John’s mother. All vital fields, spouses, children and earlier parent grades remain unchanged. The 64% is an individual comparative judgment for this entire father-profile proposition, including the profile and generation assumptions, not a measured probability.

estimates.basis: Select James Glasgow-3332 as the possible working father of the 1690 apprentice James Glasgow-4131, at 46% subjective confidence. The apprentice’s father is expressly named. His uncommon full name, weaving occupation, specific Lindsayland residence and death before 1690 strongly favour identification with the weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680. Glasgow-3332 is an existing compatible account already compared with that later Biggar weaver; prefer this qualified reuse to creating another same-name father. The overall 46% applies to identifying the named documentary father with that profile, including its unresolved adult identity; it does not express doubt about the explicit father–son wording. The supporting locality and trade are one combined identity argument, not independent proofs.
estimates.scope: Glasgow-3332’s independent identity is unresolved. Its estimated 1630/1634 birth and Biggar birthplace do not independently prove the 1680 match, and its inherited John-1086 parent and 1648 Johne child attachments cannot be used circularly to establish it. The alternative 1624 Quothquan-weaver identification is retained; that much earlier decedent is a poor father-generation fit for an ordinary 1690 apprenticeship, but the apprentice has no recorded age. Whitecastle James-1376 remains a compatible possible identity of the later weaver, potentially the same man as James-3332, with no merge. The Edinburgh weaver James-1150 remains a weaker comparison: identifying him with the master active in 1693 would conflict with the father being dead in 1690, but that master’s identity is itself inferred. The 1690 apprentice may still be the 1696 apprentice James-4114 after a cancelled first indenture; the different master and the father’s death must be reconciled before merging them. The 1696 father proposal stays unchanged. No mother, spouse or vital field is transferred or altered. James-3332’s 25% father and Robert-3407’s 23% father hypothesis remain unchanged; the two proposed sons are not proved brothers. This adds one selected profile connection, not a newly discovered son, independent source, or proved pedigree.
