estimates.basis: Select William Glasgow-1026 and Marion Glasgow-3025 as the probable intended couple of the 1681 banns, at 69% subjective confidence for the combined profile identification. William’s record-defined Kirknewton father account is established by Bessie’s 21 April 1682 baptism, about ten months later. The same uncommon full paternal name, parish and close sequence favour identifying that father with the groom. Marion-3025 is the existing local child account indexed in 1655, whose name, parish and ordinary mid-twenties adult generation make her the leading bride comparison. Prefer this qualified reuse of two compatible existing accounts to leaving the recorded couple unconnected or creating another William and Marion. This selects the intended couple; it does not prove a completed wedding or a ceremony date.
estimates.scope: The alternative explanations remain: another William could be the groom or Bessie’s father; the bride could be another Marion, including the compatible Inveresk Marion-1429/Marione-3049 or Edinburgh Marion-3143 accounts. The earlier 1664 William banns item supplies another adult-couple comparison, not proof of one man’s remarriage. The older William-1087 remains a possible groom comparison if the bride is a different Marion; Marion-3025’s own William-1087 father identification is ungraded and cannot be used circularly to exclude that possibility. William-3974’s recorded 1671 childhood makes him a poor ordinary groom comparison for 1681, without validating the older man’s estimated 1660 birth. Marion’s 11 October/4 November 1655 date discrepancy is retained. Neither a shared surname nor a presumed cousin marriage proves the couple’s ancestry. The pair and maternity share identity premises and are correlated assessments, not independent proofs or mechanically multiplied probabilities. William’s John-3610 father remains 24%; no mother is transferred to his later children, no biological father is changed, and all vital fields remain unchanged.

estimates.basis: Prefer James Glasgow-2682, the father account defined by the Edinburgh Duffe household, as the 1696 apothecary apprentice James Glasgow-4114’s probable father at 82% subjective confidence. The 1696 James and 1699 Thomas entries name their father as James Glasgow, weaver and burgess. Thomas’s maintained identification with the 13 November 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe gives an entry age of almost fifteen. The household’s James children of 16 March 1679 and 18 April 1680 fit the 1696 entry at seventeen or sixteen. Thomas is the youngest recorded son in this family, consistent with the 1699 indenture’s youngest-son description; the later recorded child, Margaret in 1691, is a daughter. This household-specific age and sibling order gives a better father-profile fit than selecting the older craftsman solely through the repeated occupational description. The James-1150 account remains compatible as another account of this same adult, not an excluded or necessarily different biological father.
estimates.scope: Scope update21October: father82% unchanged; James-2682 now has Robert-1156 probable father61%, conditional on older-weaver identity70%. The following prior scope is historical where it calls Johnne26% unchanged. The 82% assesses the complete father-profile proposition, including Thomas’s inferred apprentice-to-baptism identity and the inferred common father. These clues are related and are considered together, not multiplied as independent confirmations. Neither apprentice entry names a mother, address, father’s admission date or birth date. Another matching family remains possible. The 1679 mother’s Elizabeth/Isobell attribution is retained with its existing qualification. The 1679 and 1680 James profiles remain separate, and neither is selected as the apprentice or Jean Dobie’s husband. Isobell Duffe is not assigned as James-4114’s mother. The possible cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship remains unresolved; its father was deceased, while a same-name Edinburgh master appears in 1693. The 1691 baptism alone does not prove its father alive. James-2682’s speculative Johnne-1151 ancestry at 26%, James-1150’s probable Robert-1156 ancestry at 86%, and all vital fields are unchanged. This is a revised local selection; the live father remains blank, so the pending WikiTree action is a new father addition, not replacement of a live parent. The sibling assessment remains 79%.

estimates.basis: Fendrick’s checked 1944 abstract of the 1779 Peters Township will identifies John Glasgow’s wife Ann, daughters Lates and Agnes, and son Joseph. Glasgow-4028 and Glasgow-4029 are the existing record-defined daughter and son accounts, not speculative later adult identifications. Assess John as their father at 98% each, strongly supported by the explicit abstracted relationship and matching will context. estimates.limitations: The original will and probate packet remain uninspected. The checked abstract gives 1779, not the execution/probate days; existing 14 March and 3 September date limits are preserved from the earlier cited profile account, not newly verified. The will index verifies John’s locator, Cumberland Will Book C, p.161, but supplies no relatives. Ann is named as wife, not expressly mother of the children; her existing maternal attachments remain unassessed. Nancy (Glascoe) Wright is only a possible identification of Agnes: an approximately 1778 birth fits a child alive in 1779 and Agnes/Nancy can be compatible name forms, but the later Maryland/Indiana household has no inspected parent, guardianship or estate bridge to Peters Township. Her existing John father is therefore possible at 37%, not confident. The witness Joseph is not proved to be Joseph of Wythe County. The family-history article may depend on Faris and is not independent corroboration of his genealogy. The older James-1025 father of James-1024 remains 18%; no Scottish migration, Mary Harkness maternity, new mother, identity merge or live edit follows. Exact percentages express individual subjective judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied independent probabilities.

assessment_history.source_basis: Assess James of Moneymore, Glasgow-1024, as John of Peters Township’s probable father at 76%. The 2024 Adams County family account specifically identifies the John who died in 1779 as brother of Robert, Arthur and Joseph. Fendrick’s abstract independently supplies a contemporary Joseph Glasgow witness in John’s Peters Township will; James Neely’s presence also fits the later Neely-associated emigrant family. Faris’s catalogue description identifies Robert’s father as James of Moneymore and reports four emigrant brothers. Together these identify a specific compatible family, rather than only another local James. Extend that probable father across the preferred fourth-brother identification, while rating John lower than the three established brothers because his place in that group depends partly on the later account and witness identification. Assess the John-to-each-established-brother relationship as probable at 83%.

The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms index entry for William Glasgow, 12 June 1733 at Dundonald (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/15153407), carries a father field reading only 'Glasgow' (no forename) beside mother Barbara Stevenson. The earlier assessment rested on a Findmypast transcript with no father field at all; the Ancestry index shows a Glasgow father was indexed, which removes the objection that the 1733 baptism may have been recorded without a father. Barbara Stevenson is recorded in the catalogue as the wife of William Glasgow-3586, the weaver named in Jean's baptism of 1 October 1732 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/10876670), and the boy's name agrees with the proposed father. The father's forename is still not given, the pairing of William and Barbara is a tree pairing not traced to a marriage record, and the 254-day spacing from Jean's baptism remains unexplained, so the confidence rises only from 52% to 60% (probable). Earlier reasoning retained: Select William Glasgow-3586, the weaver at Achenyeards named as Jean’s father in the 1 October 1732 Dundonald baptism, as William Glasgow-4101’s possible father at 52% subjective confidence. The specific existing local household offers a more useful working placement than leaving the 1733 child isolated: the children share the uncommon surname and parish, their entries occur on nearby pages of the same register, and the boy’s William name agrees with the proposed father. The existing father account is already paired with Barbara Stevenson, the boy’s named mother, but that tree pairing has not been traced to an independent marriage or full-parent entry and is not counted as additional proof.
estimates.limitations: The 1733 transcript has no father field or residence; absence from a transcript does not establish what the manuscript contains or prove illegitimacy. The 1732 transcript names William, weaver at Achenyeards, but no mother. Their baptisms are only 254 days apart, about eight and a half months: close spacing weakens a routine successive-infant-birth interpretation, while unknown birth dates and possible delayed baptism leave the proposed siblings compatible. Do not manufacture birth dates to resolve it. Another Glasgow father, a different Barbara Stevenson, and two separate local families remain alternatives. Barbara’s identification with her own 1733 citation is strong; the adult couple and cross-child father assignment are separate inferences. No mother is assigned to Jean, no full-sibling claim is made, and the existing ungraded Jean-to-William father relationship is unchanged. The earlier Ayrshire William accounts Glasgow-1055, Glasgow-3288 and Glasgow-1061 remain compatible wider comparisons; estimated ages or missing family details do not exclude them. No record links this father to any of their birth families, so no upstream father is selected. No later newspaper, maritime or American identity is inferred for the child. Exact percentages are individual judgments, not measured frequencies. Original register images were not newly inspected and no live WikiTree edit is made.

Thomas’s maintained identification with the 1684 child of James and Isobell Duffe fits entry at almost fifteen. estimates.basis: James Glasgow-2682, father of the Edinburgh Duffe household, probably represents the same adult as James Glasgow-1150, the weaver apprenticed on 16 June 1641 and admitted burgess on 20 June 1649: 70% subjective identity confidence. Thomas’s maintained 1684 baptismal identification and the Duffe household’s James children of 1679 and 1680 fit those apprenticeship ages and the youngest-son order. The older craftsman independently has that specific craft and civic status, with an exact master/date cross-reference between his 1641 apprenticeship and 1649 admission. The maintained admission review found one matching admission, although this does not establish uniqueness. His marriages to Bessie Whyte on 6 July 1649 and Agnes Duncan on 11 November 1653, followed by Agnes’s burial as the weaver’s wife on 21 January 1674, permit a later Duffe household beginning in 1677. Successive marriages explain the wife sequence without requiring another same-name weaver and burgess. Select Robert Glasgow-1156 as James-2682’s probable working father at 61%, conditional on that preferred adult identity and the existing 86% identification of the 1641 apprentice’s named father Robert with the Duddingston account buried in 1647. The live father was blank in the public check on 21 October 2026: the outstanding WikiTree action is a new probable father addition, not replacement of a live father. estimates.scope: The main weaknesses are a very long working life and late fatherhood through 1691, together with the absence of a marriage, prior-wife clause, address, witness or admission-date reference directly joining the Duffe husband to the 1649 burgess. The 1693 same-name weaver master is an inferred identification, not an independently dated identity bridge. Another younger Edinburgh weaver and burgess remains possible. The cancelled 1690 Lindsayland apprenticeship could concern the 1696 son, but its deceased father would conflict with assigning that father to the living 1693 master; resolve this before a merge. Retain both James profiles as accounts of potentially one adult, not two proved sons of Robert. Johnne-1151 remains an unselected younger-family alternative at 26%, alongside the James-3076/James-3077 and Annapill Glessie childhood route, John-1084’s Gordon family, and an unrecorded father. Those alternatives are conditional on the Duffe husband being a distinct younger man, not equally compatible with the preferred pre-1641 adult.

estimates.basis: The 1712 Stichill James, explicitly indexed as Patrick Glasow and Helen Fairbarn’s son, is confidently inferred to be the James who married Elizabath Tait in the same parish in January 1740. An age of about 28, continuity in this small local surname family and the later household’s son Patrick (1742) and daughter Helen (1750), repeating both proposed paternal grandparents’ names, form a combined identity argument. Naming is supporting evidence rather than a mandatory rule or independent proof of each step. The specific Patrick/Helen household is independently established by their 1707 marriage entries and 1708–1716 children. Newly inspected printed court minutes place Patrick at Stichill in 1712 and appoint him a burlaw man in 1715; these add local continuity, not a father clause. The unsupported Uphall field is not a competing contemporary record. No concrete rival Stichill James family has been identified in the held material; this is not an exhaustive population search.

No birth, death, place, spouse, parent selection or identity merge changes. The new court pages establish recorded acts, not biological kinship. WikiTree’s father control was checked on 22 October 2026 and was already confident; no new live certainty mark is pending.

estimates.basis: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms index entry for James Glasgow, 21 May 1738 at Covington and Thankerton (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/15441533), names father George Glasgow and mother Agnes Williamson. The named couple is the catalogue couple: George Glasgow and Agnes Williamson are recorded as spouses, so the entry places the child in the household already attached. The same parents recur in the parish index: Marion 6 Apr 1740 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/26485000), Robert 12 Dec 1742 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/18855852), Agnes 23 Dec 1744 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/3769106), William Nov 1747 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/27393759), Bessie 30 Jun 1750 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/3769002). The existing 42% (possible, assessed 2026-10-22) is kept: its stated uncertainty concerns the identification of George Glasgow himself with an earlier-born person or other points outside this baptism, which a child's baptism cannot settle, so the entry is added to the basis and the percentage is not lowered. Earlier reasoning retained: James’s1738 Covington and Thankerton baptism names George Glasgow and Agnes Williamson. Selected George-1070 is the1719 Kilwinning child; fatherhood at18–19 is possible, and the existing family supplies a specific candidate. However no held record connects that child to the Covington George, and movement between Ayrshire and Lanarkshire is assumed. The child’s explicit named father does not make this particular George identification confident.
estimates.scope: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms rows are Ancestry's copy of the FamilySearch Scotland Births and Baptisms index; where the same entry was already held it is not counted twice. Index transcript only; original register uninspected. The entry gives no age, occupation or residence for the parents. Earlier limitation retained: Complete James-to-George1070 placement42%, possible. The1738 record defines a George/Agnes household; James’s later adult and his own descendants remain separate identifications. No maternal or vital change.

estimates.basis: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms index entry for Hugh Glasgow, 5 Feb 1710 at Kilwinning (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/17620473), names father John Glasgow and mother Mary Gemmill. The named couple is the catalogue couple: John Glasgow and Mary (Gemill) Glasgow are recorded as spouses, so the entry places the child in the household already attached. The same parents recur in the parish index: James 12 Mar 1707 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/11797031), Alexander 29 Nov 1710 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/10385683), Andrew 25 Jan 1712 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/26671483), Margaret 12 Sep 1714 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/8488620), Mary 25 Jul 1717 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/3283339). The existing 62% (probable, assessed 2026-10-23) is kept: its stated uncertainty concerns the identification of John Glasgow himself with an earlier-born person or other points outside this baptism, which a child's baptism cannot settle, so the entry is added to the basis and the percentage is not lowered. Earlier reasoning retained: The adult Hugh/Margaret household is established by the 1732 Kilmarnock marriage and later children. Hugh’s 1710 Kilwinning baptism, OPR 599/1 p.70, names John Glasgow and Mary Gemmill; its recorded-child parent clause retains 93% conditional confidence. A 1710 birth permits marriage at 22 and Ann’s baptism at 39, and regional proximity supports continuity. None of the held adult records names his parents or connects the glover’s occupation with the Kilwinning child, so the complete adult-to-John-1927 relationship is assessed 62%.
estimates.scope: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms rows are Ancestry's copy of the FamilySearch Scotland Births and Baptisms index; where the same entry was already held it is not counted twice. Mary Gemmill’s maternity depends on the same separate lifetime identity and is not reassessed automatically. Original register images uninspected.

estimates.basis: The 1786 Currituck Isaac account fits the exact seven-child family. The will independently names Isaac and the other six children; the later Tennessee identification is not proved by this will. The skeletal Glasgow-2363 account remains a possible duplicate. William Glasgow’s Currituck will, dated 14 October 1805 and recorded 22 January 1806, names wife Sarah, sons Caleb, Isaac, Samuel and John C., and daughters Ruth, Love Bright and Sophia. Its land divisions and household bequests identify one specific family. The named wife and all seven child names strongly identify the maintained William-357 family, with John C. compatible with John Cooper and Love now recorded under Bright; this conjunction outweighs the unsourced August death claim. The published transcription is by Judy Merrell Brickhouse, citing Currituck County Will Book 2, pp.279–280. The manuscript was not inspected. The will also transfers an enslaved boy; that clause does not add a biological family relationship.
estimates.scope: These percentages assess each existing child-to-William profile pair from the combined named household, locality and compatible generation; they are subjective, not measured frequencies. The will proves the stated father roles through a checked transcription, not the children’s exact birthdays, later migrations, spouses or descendants. Sarah is named as William’s wife, not explicitly as every child’s mother, and her Cooper maiden surname is not supplied. All maternal assessments remain separate. William’s own Caleb-363 father hypothesis stays 29%. No father is newly attached and no profile is merged. The will names one son Isaac. The 1786 Currituck child account Glascow-14 is the preferred identification within this seven-child household. Glasgow-2363, a sparsely sourced Isaac account with estimated circa-1800 birth, no spouse and an attached son Enoch, remains a compatible alternative profile mapping or possible duplicate, not a second proved son. Its existing possible father rating stays 43%; the will alone does not distinguish its identity. Enoch’s later Tennessee setting fits either comparison without proving the bridge. The differing unsourced birth estimate does not exclude it. No merge or detachment is selected.

estimates.last_test: The 1935 printed Glasgow burgess register has been visually inspected. On 14 September 1795 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as husband of Helen, lawful daughter of James Smith, mason and burgess/guild brother (printed p.197, PDF207). On 1 July 1817 Alexander Glasgow, merchant in Wilson’s Court, Argyle Street, entered as eldest son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.306, PDF316). On 3 May 1844 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as a younger son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.450, PDF460). The first entry strongly identifies the maintained John-1348/Helen Smith household; the sons are supported comparisons with Alexander-971 and John-1355. The sons’ entries do not name their mother, and the three admissions must not be treated as a literal statement that all three men form one family. These are inspected published register transcriptions; the underlying manuscript admission registers are unread. Burke’s Visitation, vol.2, printed armorial section p.67 (PDF341), has now been read in the scan. It explicitly describes Alexander of Old Court, formerly Auchinraith, as eldest son of the late John Glasgow and Helen, daughter of James Smith, and grandson of Alexander Glasgow, merchant, and Agnes Monro of Edinburgh. The family passage was already quoted in the held biography; inspecting it is not discovery of a previously unknown grandfather name. The underlying Lyon matriculation remains unread. The FamilySearch citation X17D-67M was checked directly: John was born 13 October 1771 and christened 19 October 1771 at Barony, parents Alexander Glasgow and Mary Munro. The copied 3 December 1765 date attached to that same citation is wrong; no independent 1765 record was verified in this review. This corrects the source account, not the vital fields or later identity of either modern John profile.

estimates.basis: The retained John-2871 remains the leading named father hypothesis for Hugh. The reviewed Chester tax index lists John with 80 acres in West Nottingham in 1787–1791 and Hugh with 80 acres in 1793–1799, after John’s recorded 1792 death. That consecutive name, locality and acreage pattern supports family succession, but the tax index is not a conveyance proving the same parcel or a father–son relationship. The newly inspected Gibson p. 414 names neither parent and instead says Hugh’s father emigrated about 1730 and died in 1772. Those dates conflict with John-2871’s retained 1738 birth and 1792 death. The late history may contain errors, so the existing father remains probable, but its general Nottingham context cannot be counted as independent agreement on this particular John. File 4225 independently documents a John’s 1792 East Nottingham estate; it does not name Hugh in the inspected surviving papers.

estimates.basis: The anonymous family recollection printed by Faris on p.9 explicitly gives James Glasgow, husband of Margaret Rutherford, four sons: William, Robert, James who settled near Moneymore, and Samuel who went to America, plus daughter Ellen. The letter-defined father is the family role represented by James-1025. These are specific named relationships, substantially stronger than the contributed-tree and locality summaries used by the earlier percentages. The same full-letter tradition was already read on 20 October; actual Faris pages now confirm its full structure. Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses. William-2426 already represents the letter’s maternal-grandfather family role and is assessed as Margaret, wife of the Coleraine minister’s father at 84%. The same letter explicitly names his own father James and mother Margaret Rutherford. Reconcile this previously underused explicit relationship at 84%; do not transfer it to the distinct Cunningham husband or treat the imported circa1829 United States death as established. These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris calls the anonymous recollection file5 within PRONI T1959, while Rutherford’s reproduced copy cites T1959/3; retain this reference discrepancy pending archive checking. The 1759 probate index says Drumcarn and names no kin; neither that testator nor the inherited life dates are identified by this reassessment. The letter calls William eldest although the imported sibling birth estimates put him later; those estimates remain unverified. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed.

estimates.basis: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms index entry for John Glasgow, 6 July 1786 at Eccles, Berwickshire (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/27458592), reads the parent fields that the previous review could not see: father Robert and mother Agnes (forenames only). The previous 49% rested only on a handed-down family tree that quotes no record. John's birth date 6 July 1786 is exactly this entry, and the index shows one Robert and Agnes family at Eccles (which includes Leitholm) from 1779 to 1795: James 1779, Thomas 1781, Marion 1782, William 1784, John 1786, Agnes 1789, Thomas 1791 and Isobel 1795 (for example https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/27458082). That is the household of Robert Glasgow-3706 and Agnes Whitehead, who married at Leitholm in 1779. Confidence rises from 49% to 85% probable.
estimates.scope: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms rows are Ancestry's copy of the FamilySearch Scotland Births and Baptisms index already cited, so they verify the indexed parent fields rather than adding an independent source; the original register is uninspected. The index row gives the mother's forename only; Whitehead comes from the couple's 1779 marriage. John's later identity as the Leitholm man who died in 1864 rests on his profile's birth date and residence. Robert-3706's own father link (James-1238, 34%) is separate and unchanged. No mother change follows.

Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses. This specific position in the named sibling family supports 77%, while his adult life remains little anchored. His imported United States death location is not established by the letter or by the will’s Ireland designation. These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed.

estimates.basis: The actual Faris book has now been inspected, rather than only its catalogue abstract. Printed p.11 uses a dotted possible connection from James of Moneymore to the American brothers; p.12 explicitly reports that evidence for Robert and his brothers’ parentage had not been found. James was the author’s identifiable County Londonderry candidate, not an evidenced father. The retrospective Irish pedigree on pp.8–9 and Samuel’s 1824 Pennsylvania will discussed on p.12 identify an Irish sibling group, including William, James and Robert remaining in Ireland, without joining it to the emigrant brothers. County setting, a compatible generation and the existing family tradition keep James a plausible candidate, but cannot sustain the earlier probable father assessment. Mary’s case additionally depends on identifying the 1779 will witness Mary Arter as the emigrant sister. Faris p.13 transmits an unnamed sister styled Mrs Arthur; p.15 identifies Mary Arter with that sister through the tax/probate cluster, rather than an explicit sibling or birth statement. The association remains positive but does not establish her father. Robert, Arthur and Joseph’s established brotherhood remains separately supported by the maintained 1806 letter transcription and Joseph’s 1831 will. John of Peters Township remains a probable brother at 83%; Faris p.15 also reconstructs the four brothers from the 1779–1780 tax/probate cluster. These sibling arguments do not identify their father. The 1824 Samuel will has been read only through Faris’s excerpt, not its manuscript. The Irish Robert in that will/pedigree is not identified as the emigrant Robert born in 1749. All mothers, upstream ancestry, life dates and current attachments are preserved; no live WikiTree save or identity merge follows. Exact percentages are subjective pair-specific judgments, not measured frequencies or multiplied probabilities.

estimates.basis: The named son Caleb matches the established eldest Currituck child account and his six co-listed siblings, not just a repeated Caleb name. William Glasgow’s Currituck will, dated 14 October 1805 and recorded 22 January 1806, names wife Sarah, sons Caleb, Isaac, Samuel and John C., and daughters Ruth, Love Bright and Sophia. Its land divisions and household bequests identify one specific family. The named wife and all seven child names strongly identify the maintained William-357 family, with John C. compatible with John Cooper and Love now recorded under Bright; this conjunction outweighs the unsourced August death claim. The published transcription is by Judy Merrell Brickhouse, citing Currituck County Will Book 2, pp.279–280. The manuscript was not inspected. The will also transfers an enslaved boy; that clause does not add a biological family relationship.
estimates.scope: These percentages assess each existing child-to-William profile pair from the combined named household, locality and compatible generation; they are subjective, not measured frequencies. The will proves the stated father roles through a checked transcription, not the children’s exact birthdays, later migrations, spouses or descendants. Sarah is named as William’s wife, not explicitly as every child’s mother, and her Cooper maiden surname is not supplied. All maternal assessments remain separate. William’s own Caleb-363 father hypothesis stays 29%. No father is newly attached and no profile is merged.

That is the catalogue couple: Alexander Glasgow-1321 and his tree spouse Agnes (Cunningham) Glasgow, whose other children belong to the same 1774-1777 Edinburgh household. The 22 Oct 2026 assessment (59%, possible) rested on the generic OPR citation and said the absent literal fields left material uncertainty; those fields are now read and name exactly this father and mother. The raise is modest, to 63% (probable, the lower edge), because a child's baptism cannot show that this Edinburgh Alexander is the Kirknewton-born Alexander-1321 (born before 1747) or choose between the two Agnes Cunningham profiles (Cunningham-20926 and the draft Cunninghame-96).

estimates.basis: The distinctive daughter Love, recorded as Bright, matches the Currituck Love account and its six siblings. The will establishes her married surname by October 1805, but does not identify her husband; witness Isaac Bright is not automatically assigned as husband. William Glasgow’s Currituck will, dated 14 October 1805 and recorded 22 January 1806, names wife Sarah, sons Caleb, Isaac, Samuel and John C., and daughters Ruth, Love Bright and Sophia. Its land divisions and household bequests identify one specific family. The named wife and all seven child names strongly identify the maintained William-357 family, with John C. compatible with John Cooper and Love now recorded under Bright; this conjunction outweighs the unsourced August death claim. The published transcription is by Judy Merrell Brickhouse, citing Currituck County Will Book 2, pp.279–280. The manuscript was not inspected. The will also transfers an enslaved boy; that clause does not add a biological family relationship.
estimates.scope: These percentages assess each existing child-to-William profile pair from the combined named household, locality and compatible generation; they are subjective, not measured frequencies. The will proves the stated father roles through a checked transcription, not the children’s exact birthdays, later migrations, spouses or descendants. Sarah is named as William’s wife, not explicitly as every child’s mother, and her Cooper maiden surname is not supplied. All maternal assessments remain separate. William’s own Caleb-363 father hypothesis stays 29%. No father is newly attached and no profile is merged.

The will also transfers an enslaved boy; that clause does not add a biological family relationship.

estimates.scope: 96% is a subjective confident assessment of the complete father–child identity. Huston is the source form; Robert Houston is the compatible profile. estimates.basis: Select John Glasgow-1022 as the possible working father of the Glenleslie Robert represented by Glasgow-1367, at 38% subjective confidence. The original makes their reported age difference 28 years (100 versus 72), a comfortable father–son interval. They were Antrim-born Glasgow farmers in Glenleslie households 21 and 23, separated by the Hamill household. This is a specific nearby older family, and John is the best identified local father comparison already retained in the research. Reading the original marriage question removes the previous overstatement that it expressly records a first marriage in 1791. The combined generation and neighbouring-family argument is sufficient to select a weak working model rather than leave this preferred named comparison outside the tree; it is not a parent statement.
estimates.scope: 38% assesses the complete John-to-Robert profile hypothesis, not the certainty of reading the census. Robert’s census-implied birth about 1778–1779 precedes the sole reported marriage year by roughly twelve years. An earlier union, nonmarital fatherhood or a reporting error would still be needed, and none is established. The original asks for multiple marriage years, so omission of an earlier year remains a real limitation. John’s exceptional age may be inaccurate. An uncle, cousin, other collateral relative or unrepresented father remains possible; the older Alexander comparison is not excluded. Rose’s reported age does not fit her as Robert’s mother, and no mother or earlier wife is assigned. The selection concerns the 1851 Glenleslie man only: it does not identify him with the Lisnagaver tithe occupier, validate every attached child, or prove a Y-DNA pedigree. Hugh-3956’s 74% brother hypothesis includes a separate identity uncertainty and is not automatically assigned this father; his estimated earlier generation also needs its own chronology test. The inherited Unknown Glasgow-3905 is preserved as an uncertain alternative with no invented percentage. No live WikiTree family field is changed.
estimates.last_test: Held explicit census relatives, Hugh’s Mary-based sibling argument and Robert’s will family compared against John–Robert proposition; no overlooked paternal bridge.
estimates.next_test: Seek a tenancy succession or church/family instrument naming Robert and Andrew/Hugh as sons of the same John; alternatively identify census-nephew John’s father through his actual1839 marriage and a Glenleslie locator.

estimates.basis: Thomas is the probable working father of Roanoke Joseph Glasgow-2573 at 74%. The inspected 1877 Campbell original explicitly names Thomas and Rose Glasgo as parents of Jos. Glasgo and records J. Glasgo, Son, as informant. The 1866 cohabitation-register-derived account identifies Joe, Lucy Gilbert and nine children. The younger Joseph’s held 1878 marriage and 1880/1900 Campbell households supply a plausible family continuation, supporting the existing identification of the elder Joseph’s Campbell death. Its conflicting birthplace, age and Unmarried entry remain unresolved. Parent names already appeared in the biography; this is a qualified structured father selection, not newly discovered names or a merger of existing branches. The original 1877 entry gives age 80 and a ditto Campbell birthplace, whereas the Roanoke account gives Richmond and the 1870 census age 80 implies about 1790. Its consort column repeats Unmarried rather than naming Lucy. The informant is J. Glasgo, designated Son, without a full forename. The younger Joseph’s 1914 certificate clearly names mother Lucy Gilbert, but its father abbreviation remains ambiguous Jas./Jos.; independent readings prefer Jas., and the father’s birthplace is uncertain, tentatively Fredericktown, Md. It does not resolve the 1877 deceased’s identity or name Thomas. Census and marriage household accounts are reused captures, not freshly inspected images. Companion death indexes concern the same event. No existing numbered Thomas, marriage to Rose, older Glasgow lineage or common Y-DNA origin is established.

estimates.basis: Samuel-2872 is now identified with the 1824 West Fallowfield testator at 98% subjective confidence: his checked memorial names both wives Judith and Tabitha and the infant daughter Margaret Ellen, matching the original will. The newly inspected official deed index places Samuel in West Fallowfield and enters Judith Heslett in the spouse column in 1805 and 1812, with repeated Haslett dealings. These connect the already recorded Judith household to the later Tabitha estate. The will names the testator’s three brothers William, James and Robert Glasgow of Ireland; the anonymous Irish family recollection names those same three brothers with Samuel, who went to America, as children of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford. The distinctive sibling constellation and transatlantic division favour this particular Irish father over the current John reconstruction. The 98% testator identification does not prove his father. 67% is a combined subjective father-profile judgement, not a multiplication of independent probabilities. Repeated family names can occur in another generation. The memorial contributes a 1761 Pennsylvania birth and a John father attribution, but no underlying birth or Bible entry has been inspected. These remain substantive competing claims. The letter account’s estimated 1726 Samuel birth, Margaret Rutherford’s estimated 1700 birth and James’s supposed 1759 death are consequential conflicts if established; no date is adjusted to force the preferred route. The 1759 Drumcarn testator’s identification with James-1025 remains unproved. Samuel-1492 remains the separate letter-defined account, father 76%, with possible duplicate identity, not a proved second son or a merge. Mary Cranmer’s existing maternal attachment is not reassessed or transferred to Margaret Rutherford. The current Find a Grave family links and the compiled Bible narrative are claims, not inspected original parent entries. The deed originals remain unread; Judith Heslett is the index’s spouse-column wording, not an established maiden surname.
estimates.scope: Preferred replacement father James Glasgow-1025, 67% probable, for Samuel Glasgow-2872; John Glasgow-2870 retained as an unselected 25% uncertain alternative, previously 72% probable. No mother, vital date, person merge or live attachment is changed.

estimates.basis: Joseph Glasgow-1543 is selected as a possible biological father of William Glasgow-3678 at 30% subjective confidence. The published 1831 will names a William Glasgow who was raised by Joseph and leaves remaining property to that William’s children. The local William/Sally household, William’s circa 1788 birth and Joseph’s birth before 1765 permit fatherhood; the unnamed 1810 Wythe male 16–25 is compatible. The newly read 1829 original confirms this married William locally but names no parent. This is an explicit working inference from a specific caregiving and testamentary family context, not a literal parent statement. Two propositions remain unresolved: which William the will means, and whether upbringing denotes biological sonship. William Glasgow-563, born 1778, Robert-12’s son, married 1802 with children born 1803–1822, is a substantive compatible alternative will subject; Ohio residence from 1805 does not exclude earlier upbringing or a legacy. William P. Glasgow-559, born 1813, has a later known family and is a weaker comparison, not categorically excluded. The will names no wife or residence for William. It explicitly calls Arthur’s son Robert a nephew and gives him the real-estate balance and furniture; William’s children receive the remaining property, not the whole estate. A nephew or another related dependent remains a strong alternative to biological sonship. The 1810 young man is unnamed. No mother, vital date, original tree or live WikiTree attachment is changed. estimates.basis: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Marriages index entry for 5 March 1754 at Falkirk records Jean Glasgow marrying John and names her father as George Glasgow. Jean Glasgow-810's account already gives exactly this marriage: 5 March 1754, to John Renny, writer and later bailie of Falkirk, whose 1809 estate settlement names their daughters. Date, parish and the husband's forename all agree, so the bride is very probably Jean-810. Her previously unknown father is therefore attached as George Glasgow, the record-defined draft record-ancestry-glasgow-0c9011a8adf0, at 80% probable.
estimates.scope: Search-result index row only: relatives appear as forenames, so the father's surname is inferred from the bride's, and reading George as her father follows the collection's father-then-spouse pattern confirmed by full parent rows elsewhere in the same index (for example record 1009144). The original Falkirk register entry has not been inspected, and Ancestry's index shares its Old Parish Register indexing with other providers, so their copies are not independent. No existing catalogue George fits Falkirk: George-1058 (Kilwinning), George-3966 (Ireland), George-4165 (Irvine) and the 1724 court-file George remain unexcluded comparisons, not identifications, and the draft is not merged with any of them. Jean's birth about 1733 is an estimate from the marriage. No mother is inferred.

estimates.basis: Ancestry's England, Select Births and Christenings index records William, son of William Alexander Glasgow and Elizabeth Rachel, baptised 23 July 1815 at Berwick-upon-Tweed; William Brown Glasgow-1001's account gives exactly that date and place. The England, Select Marriages index records the 9 March 1862 Kendal marriage of William Glasgow, aged 44, to Margaret Ward, naming his father as William Alexander Glasgow; William Brown Glasgow was then living at Kendal, and children John Harrison (1862) and Joseph Alexander (1864) were baptised there to William (Brown) Glasgow and Margaret, so the 1862 groom is William-1001 remarrying after Dinah. A third index entry records William Alexander Glasgow marrying Elizabeth Rachel Brown at Berwick on 24 December 1810, which explains William's middle name Brown. Two separate registers, 47 years apart, name the same distinctive father, so William Alexander Glasgow (record-defined draft record-ancestry-glasgow-04d267d61354) is attached at 85% probable.
estimates.scope: Index transcripts only (FamilySearch-derived); the Berwick and Kendal registers are uninspected. The 1862 age 44 implies about 1818, three years later than the 1815 baptism, a common remarriage understatement. The 1845 Kendal marriage index for William Brown Glasgow and Dinah Bell gives his father as 'William Brown', read here as a truncated or garbled entry rather than a different father; it is kept as a stated discrepancy. The 1810 Berwick groom is not Glasgow-3324 of Larne (died there in 1816, wife Elizabeth Stewart); Scottish index entries at Montrose for Joseph Brown Glasgow (1817) and Rachael Glasgow (1824), children of William Alexander and Elizabeth Rachael, suggest the family moved to Angus, but are not yet linked. William Alexander's own parentage is unknown. No mother is assessed here.

estimates.basis: Robert Glasgow-2866, iron founder and bachelor, married Mary Ann Anthony by licence at Manchester Collegiate Church on 16 September 1834 (his biography's register extract; England, Select Marriages index entry). The witnesses were Annie Glasgow, Agnes Glasgow and William Glasgow: the names of William Glasgow-3545, his wife Ann (Denham) and their daughter Agnes-3544. The Lloyd Street Presbyterian Chapel baptised a Robert, born 5 September 1806, to William and Ann Glasgow, the first child after William and Ann's 1805 Manchester marriage. Robert-2866 is therefore very probably that son, and William-3545 is attached as his father at 70% probable.
estimates.scope: Index transcripts and a contributed register extract; originals uninspected. Witnesses suggest but do not state kinship, and several other Robert Glasgows (with Martha, Jane and Lucy Gatliff) were having children in Manchester in the 1830s. Robert-2866's 'about 1815' birth is only an estimate; the 1806 baptism, if his, puts him at 28 at marriage. The record-defined draft for the 1806 baptism (record-ancestry-glasgow-f0367a88c291) is probably the same man and should be consolidated with Robert-2866. No mother is assessed.

Birth and marriage registers agree on the father, so James Glasgow of Sunderland, husband of Jane Clough Duncan (record-defined draft record-ancestry-glasgow-fd84e4728b02), is attached at 88% probable.
estimates.scope: Index transcripts only; the Sunderland and Bishopwearmouth registers are uninspected. The indexing pipeline's possible link of the 1852 marriage's father to James Glasgow-1701 of Killycurragh, County Tyrone, has no support beyond the name and is not adopted. Other Sunderland Glasgow fathers (John, Peter) are distinct couples. James's own birth and parentage are unknown. Mother Jane Clough Duncan is named but not assessed here.

estimates.basis: The Ancestry India, Select Deaths and Burials index records Eliza Corbitt Glasgow, aged 0, buried at Rajkot, Bombay, on 27 May 1845, with her father indexed as 'A.D Glasgow' (record 310212, and the paired father entry 310211). Adam Dickie Glasgow-1781 (born 1815 at Lisburn) is the only catalogue Glasgow with those initials, and his brother, the missionary James McClure Glasgow-1780, was at Rajkot that year: James's daughter Jane Henrie Glasgow-2899 was buried there on 14 April 1845 in the same register. Eliza is therefore attached to Adam Dickie Glasgow as a probable father at 70%.
estimates.scope: Index transcript only (FamilySearch's India burial index via Ancestry); the Bombay ecclesiastical return is uninspected. The father is given by initials only, and Adam Dickie Glasgow's own presence in India in 1845 is not independently documented here; a different A. D. Glasgow attached to the Irish Presbyterian mission is not excluded. Eliza is a record-defined draft (record-ancestry-glasgow-cb7d30031f5e). No mother is inferred.

estimates.basis: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Marriages index records Susan Glasgow marrying John on 17 July 1826 at St Cuthbert's, Edinburgh, and a separate parent row in the same index names William Glasgow as father of Susan Glasgow. Susanna (Glasgow) McIntosh-895's account gives the same marriage, to John McIntosh on 17 July 1826 at St Cuthbert's, so the bride identity is strong. William Glasgow, the record-defined draft record-ancestry-glasgow-c615b38b160b, is added as her possible father at 55%.
estimates.scope: Her biography instead calls her the daughter of Colin Glasgow and Margaret Fraser of Clackmannan, without a cited source (perhaps family tradition or her 1862 New South Wales death registration, which has not been inspected). The two named fathers conflict and neither is excluded: the contemporary marriage index is preferred, but held at possible because of that conflict. Search-result and parent index rows only; the original St Cuthbert's register is uninspected. No catalogue William is identified with the draft; William-2965, William-563, William-2130 and others remain unexcluded comparisons. No Colin profile is created and no mother is inferred.

estimates.basis: Alexander Glasgow-2695, the Midlothian agricultural labourer/ploughman, reports Colinton (also rendered Callington) as his birthplace, with census-implied births about 1801–1803. Alexander Glasgow-2718 was born 17 March 1799 and baptised 31 March at Colinton, residence Greysmill, explicitly to John Glasgow and Margaret Muckle. The distinctive birth parish, compatible two-to-four-year census age discrepancy and the family’s later Kirknewton context support identifying the childhood and adult accounts. John/Margaret’s recorded children at Kirknewton and East Calder in 1808–1814 provide a positive locality bridge to adult Alexander’s son John, born at Kirknewton about 1829. The first held son’s name John is only a minor, correlated clue. A bounded FamilySearch search for Alexander Glasgow, Colinton, 1795–1806 in Scotland Births and Baptisms returned the 1799child and two occurrences of the adult as a father; no closer childhood candidate was returned. This supports selecting the record-defined John Glasgow-1304 as the adult’s father at 65% subjective confidence, a new working attachment rather than a profile merger.
estimates.scope: No inspected adult record explicitly names his parents; childhood-to-adult identity is inferred. The two-to-four-year age difference remains, and the bounded selected-localities birth index is incomplete: an unindexed Colinton child or a different adult identity for the 1799child could overturn the link. The census facts are held profile/index accounts, not newly read original images. The1799provider transcript was inspected earlier, original register uninspected. The Kirknewton Meikle entries are compatible family context, not independent proof of the adult identity. John-1304 represents the named Muckle father; his internally conflicting 1765/1771/c1790 childhood estimates and 78% upstream father assessment remain unresolved and unchanged. No mother attachment, exact birth replacement, wife identity resolution, or merger of 2695 and 2718 is proposed. The 1827blacksmith’s age 14/SouthLeith index details favour a separate person and do not establish the ploughman’s parentage.

estimates.basis: George Glasgow-638 is already described in his held and live biography as the Crawford child of William Glasgow and Janet Thomson, but neither parent profile is attached. The inspected Scotland baptism index names that exact couple for George, born 8 June 1818 and baptised 14 June at Crawford. An exact-parent search returned thirteen Crawford entries spanning 1802–1828, including Isabel in 1808 and an older George in 1810. The inspected monumental-inscription transcript identifies William Glasgow-2715, gamekeeper to the Earl of Hopetoun, his wife Janet Thomson, their daughter Isabel (died 1881 aged 73), and an older George who died in July 1816. The 1841 census transcript places gamekeeper William with Janet and Isabella at Hass, Crawford; the 1851 transcript gives widower William, 72, born Crawford, with daughter Isabella and younger children. This combination supports the gamekeeper as the 1818 child’s father, with reuse of the deceased child’s name. The proposed attachment to the later Leicester adult is assessed at 88% subjective confidence, including the unresolved childhood-to-adult identification.
estimates.scope: The baptism and census originals and gravestone image have not been inspected; these are provider index/transcript readings. His inspected 1843 GRO marriage index locates a Leicester entry with Mary Ann Norton among the same-page spouse possibilities, but gives no father or father’s occupation. The original marriage is the decisive next test. The memorial’s older George, died 1816 aged 7, cannot be the 1818 child; its reported age differs by about a year from the 1810 baptism and remains unresolved. Some sibling index birth fields contain malformed years and the 1806 John dates conflict; none is silently corrected. William Glasgow-1533, the circa-1795 Glasgow-born weaver with a Janet Thomson wife, remains a distinct comparison rather than being excluded merely for missing fields: the gamekeeper’s 1841/1851 Crawford household, older age, trade, wife and Isabel chronology provide the positive match. No exact vital replacement, mother attachment, profile merger or upstream father is inferred.

estimates.basis: The 18% proposal treated James Glasgow-1144’s named son John as positive support for John of Cross. The held South Carolina transcriptions identify a separate documented son-role: the 1817 complaint names John among James and Mary’s children, Robert’s sworn answer calls himself James’s oldest son, and Mary’s 5 April 1822 Newberry will puts her son John in charge of her property and care during her life. These records favour a John active in that South Carolina household; they do not identify the Bannside weaver married to Jean McClure. The current Newberry family account represents that son as Glasgow-1146. Its gravestone-derived circa-1756 birth conflicts with Robert’s oldest-son statement and must not be used as a conclusive exclusion of the Cross man. Reassess the complete Cross-to-James father hypothesis at 8% uncertain: compatible generation and broad Antrim origin remain, but the named-son match is not an established bridge. Keep the tentative working attachment for testing; no existing person is detached.
estimates.scope: 8% is a subjective comparative assessment, not a calibrated probability. Transcriptions inspected, not the original wills, complaint, answer or memorial. Mary’s direction implies practical care but does not explicitly state John’s residence; an absent manager or return migration remains possible. No record calls the Cross John James’s son. The 1756/1762 birth-order conflict in the Newberry family remains open; this review neither resolves it nor changes John-1146’s recorded father assessment. A second living son John is possible but unsupported. James-1509, John-4179 and other fathers remain comparisons, without a new selection. The diary keyword pass found no relevant earlier kin clause and is not an exhaustive search of D2003.

estimates.basis: Grant’s inspected 1899 Edinburgh testament index, printed p.106 (PDF p.116), entry dated 3 February 1733, explicitly names James Glasgow, weaver and burgess of Edinburgh, and James Glasgow, surgeon aboard H.M. sloop Surf, his son by deceased Isobel Duff. The named parental couple and the father’s specific craft/civic status fit the existing Edinburgh Duffe household, Glasgow-2682 and Duffe-18. Glasgow-4124 is the existing account of James Glasgow, Saltoun, surgeon of Swift of Sheerness in 1733, indexed by David Dobson from SRO.S/H. The uncommon name/profession combination, same year and closely resembling vessel names strongly identify the record surgeon with that account. The independent indexed Isobel Duff relict entry dated 4 April 1733 (printed p.81/PDF p.91) fits the same parental household. The proposed father and mother are each assessed at 95% subjective confidence. Both assessments share the same surgeon identity inference; they are not independent confirmations. Public WikiTree readback on 30 October 2026 and the current local account both have no parent listed for Glasgow-4124, so this is a genuine new family connection, not grading of an existing parent.
estimates.scope: Printed index inspected, not the original 1733 testament. Surf in Grant and Swift in Dobson are retained literal variants; vessel identity has not been settled from naval records. Dobson’s SRO.S/H is a Services of Heirs reference, not an inspected original or a naval muster. No exact birth, death date, or birthplace is inferred from a register date, relict wording or Saltoun association. The surgeon is not merged with apprentice Glasgow-4114 or either 1679/1680 childhood James. James-2682’s father remains 61%, older-weaver identity 70%, and apprentice father/mother 82%/72%. Maternity is explicit for the indexed surgeon; assigning that surgeon to Glasgow-4124 is the common 95% identity bridge.

estimates.basis: Renwick's abstract of protocol 1196 (31 December 1534) records William Glasgow and Esbell Brade conveying property to their son John, with Janet Spreull as John's spouse. Both grantors are named as John's parents in the same act, so Esbell Brade, matched to Isobel (Brade) Glasgow (Brade-232, wife of William Glasgow-1098), is his mother. The 1564 protocol 805 separately makes John heir of William his father, so the parental couple is consistent. Assessed as 92% proved, separately from the father link.
estimates.scope: Printed abstract only (Renwick, Abstracts of Protocols vol. 4, protocol 1196, p. 72); the original protocol book is uninspected. The abstract names Esbell Brade by forename and surname, so identity with Brade-232 rests on that name and on her being William-1098's wife; the form Esbell/Isobel is a variant. The act does not name any other child.

estimates.basis: The Ancestry Scotland, Select Births and Baptisms index entry for Andrew Glasgow, 19 Oct 1731 at Kirknewton and East Calder (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/19991471), names father James Glasgow. Two Kirknewton men named James Glasgow are in the catalogue. James Glasgow-3526 (b. 1688) has the Helen (1714) and John (1717) baptisms at 97% and would have been 43 in 1731; James Glasgow-1547 (baptised 9 Sep 1702, son of Andrew Glasgow-1546, assessed 99%) would have been 29, and a son named Andrew follows the Scottish custom of naming the first son for the father's father. A further son Robert, baptised before 13 Feb 1735 at Kirknewton, is assigned to James-1547 at 57%, so a 1731 Andrew fits his childbearing years. On naming pattern and age James-1547 is slightly the better fit, but the entry gives no mother, residence or occupation and the two cannot be separated; the 38% (possible) leaves roughly as much weight on James-3526 and on a third man.

Assessed at 85% (probable).
estimates.scope: Ancestry index transcript only; the original register entry has not been inspected, and the provider rows are Ancestry's copy of the FamilySearch/OPR index, so duplicate rows for one event are not counted as independent. The father draft also holds a 23 Jul 1720 Mid Calder marriage of an Alexander Glasgow with no spouse indexed; a man marrying in 1720 is unlikely to father a child in 1777, so that record probably belongs to another Alexander and the draft conflates two men. The Findmypast and Ancestry transcripts share one underlying index.

estimates.basis: George Mark Glasgow is a unique full name in the Royal Artillery (2nd Lt 1824-25, Second Captain 1837, Captain 1843). If this profile is that officer, the Spectator's 'son of the late General Glasgow, of the same corps' makes him the son of Lt-Gen George Glasgow (d. 1820). The profile (c. 1805, 'British Isles', Captain, father of Madeline, dead by 1846) is a strong compatible RA candidate, but its identity conflicts with the Kingston man of 1851 (Glasgow-3785).
estimates.scope: Only one George Mark Glasgow is known in the Royal Artillery, so Glasgow-3127 and Glasgow-3785 cannot both be that officer unless the profiles are duplicates; if they are the same man the two links should be merged with the profiles. Assessed low because the identification of this profile with the officer is itself unproved. The cited records (added 5 Nov 2026) are the proposed father's records that place him in time and place; none of them names this child.

estimates.basis: The Belfast News-Letter of 20 May 1834, p. 3, and the Freeman's Journal of 23 May 1834 report the death at New Orleans on 26 Nov 1833 of Benjamin Glasgow, surgeon (formerly of Vera Cruz), 'son of the late Robert Glasgow of Cookstown, County Tyrone'. The notice names the father, so a father named Robert exists; which catalogue Robert he is is the open question. Glasgow-3941 (Robert Glasgow, Coltrim near Cookstown, leaseholder 1820-1831 and head of an eleven-person household in 1831) is the nearest adult Robert alive in the 1820s who could be dead by 1834. The other Cookstown Robert in the catalogue, Glasgow-2656 of Tullyveagh, died on 20 Aug 1856 and is excluded.
estimates.scope: The surgeon's own identification with Glasgow-3412 is 'probable', not proved. Glasgow-3941 is only one of several unprofiled Roberts (Robert of Loy is another); nothing ties Benjamin to Coltrim. The 1831 freeholder entry that places Robert alive that year is itself only a possible match. Kept at 20% as a tentative candidate for the record's father. The cited records (added 5 Nov 2026) are the child's own records that the inference rests on; none of them names this father.

estimates.basis: The Spectator of 1 March 1851 announces the death at Kingston, Canada West, of George Mark Glasgow, late Captain Royal Artillery, 'son of the late General Glasgow, of the same corps'. Only one General Glasgow served in the Royal Artillery, Lt-Gen George Glasgow (c. 1756, d. 28 Oct 1820), who was at Quebec from October 1794, when Glasgow-3785 was born there on 15 Feb 1795. The catalogue draft for the senior Royal Artillery officer George Glasgow (record-queue-newspapers-irish-1800-1850-george-senior-artillery) is that officer. Name, corps, place and date all agree.
estimates.scope: No baptism has been inspected (the Quebec Anglican register for 1795 is the test). The link of the 1851 notice to Glasgow-3785 depends on the profile's own Quebec birth and Kingston death, whose death date (6 Jan 1851) differs from the notice (26th, apparently February 1851). Glasgow-3127 (c. 1805) may be the same Royal Artillery man or a rival. The cited records (added 5 Nov 2026) are the child's own records that the inference rests on; none of them names this father.

estimates.basis: Elizabeth left a will proved at Drumgreenagh in 1812 (PRONI index), with birth given as before 1794. Glasgow-4031, John Glasgow, a Drumgreenagh farmer, and his wife Jane Murphy are named in a Registry of Deeds memorial of 13 February 1786 (registered 1792), which makes him the only dated Drumgreenagh household head of the generation that could be the parent. The surname, the single townland and the span of years fit; nothing else is known of Elizabeth Glasgow's family.
estimates.scope: No record names a parent or sibling of this person. Nathaniel Glasgow-4014 (Drumgreenagh, probate 1809, deed witness, no wife known) is an equally placed older man and could be the father instead, or John's brother or father; Glasgow-4018 (Robert, before 1818) belongs to the next generation. The deed gives no children. The cited records (added 5 Nov 2026) are the proposed father's records that place him in time and place; none of them names this child.

estimates.basis: The Leadhills Cemetery inscription (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/62497/records/370987) commemorates Janet Thomson, spouse of William Glasgow, gamekeeper to the Earl of Hopetoun (d. 1 Apr 1845 aged 62), three of her children (John and James in infancy; George d. 21 Jul 1816 aged 7), William Glasgow (d. 26 Apr 1853 aged 71) and then Isabel Glasgow (d. 27 Nov 1881 aged 73). Crawford parish (which includes Leadhills) baptised John on 7 Oct 1804 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/13623118) and George on 29 Apr 1810 (https://www.ancestry.co.uk/search/collections/60143/records/13621035) to William Glasgow and Janet Thomson, matching the infant John and the boy George on the stone. Catalogue William Glasgow-2715 (c. 1779, Crawford) has a wife Janet (Thomson) Glasgow. Isabel, born about 1808 (between the 1804 and 1810 baptisms), is placed last on the family stone, unmarried by name, which makes her most likely a daughter.
estimates.scope: The stone does not state a relationship for Isabel; she could be a daughter-in-law or another relative, and no baptism for Isabel has been found. The indexed ages put William's birth about 1782, three years after the catalogue c. 1779, which is an estimate on the profile. Index transcript of the inscription only.
